cards.title: Wittenberg

source.name: University of Wittenberg
source.citation: Founded 1502; Martin Luther posted his Ninety-five Theses there in 1517, igniting the Protestant Reformation. Also the university of the legendary Doctor Faustus (Marlowe, c. 1592).

cards.summary_basic: Wittenberg was a German university famous as the cradle of the Protestant Reformation — Martin Luther taught there and launched his challenge to the Catholic Church from it in 1517. Hamlet and Horatio are students there. For Shakespeare's audience this quietly codes Hamlet as a modern, Protestant, intellectual young man — which sits in pointed tension with a Ghost who seems to come from Catholic Purgatory.
cards.detail_scholar: Wittenberg was also the fictional university of Doctor Faustus, the over-reaching scholar of Marlowe's play; the association tinges Hamlet's bookishness with a hint of dangerous intellect. Claudius's wish that Hamlet not 'go back to Wittenberg' is thus also a wish to keep him under the court's eye, away from independent thought.

cards.title: Purgatory

source.name: Catholic doctrine; English Reformation
source.citation: Defined at the Councils of Florence (1439) and Trent (1545–63); repudiated by the Church of England in the Thirty-nine Articles (Article XXII; drafted 1563, enacted by Parliament 1571).

cards.summary_basic: In Catholic theology, Purgatory is an intermediate state after death where souls are purged of their sins by fire before they can enter heaven. The Ghost describes exactly this — 'confined to fast in fires, / till the foul crimes done in my days of nature / are burnt and purged away.' The catch: Protestant England had officially abolished Purgatory decades earlier, so a ghost claiming to come from it was theologically suspect — possibly a devil in disguise, which is why Hamlet must test its word.
cards.detail_scholar: This doctrinal fault line is central to the play's tension. A Reformation audience could not take the Ghost's origin at face value; the Protestant position held that such apparitions were demonic deceptions. Hamlet's demand for proof ('The play's the thing / Wherein I'll catch the conscience of the king') is, among other things, a theologically prudent response to an un-Protestant ghost.

cards.title: Saint Patrick and Purgatory

source.name: Medieval legend of St Patrick's Purgatory
source.citation: St Patrick's Purgatory, a pilgrimage cave on Station Island, Lough Derg, Ireland; legend made St Patrick the keeper of an entrance to Purgatory (widely current from the 12th century).

cards.summary_basic: Saint Patrick is the patron saint of Ireland, but medieval legend also made him the keeper of Purgatory — a cave said to be an entrance to the place of purging fire. Hamlet swears 'by Saint Patrick' immediately after meeting a ghost who has come from exactly that place. The oath is not random: it points straight at where the Ghost says it suffers.
cards.detail_scholar: The choice of saint is pointed wit at a tense moment: of all the saints Hamlet could swear by, he picks the one associated with Purgatory, just after the Ghost has described purgatorial fires. It is one of several signals that Hamlet has grasped — and is privately turning over — the Ghost's claimed origin.

cards.title: The Vice of the morality plays

source.name: Spivack, Shakespeare and the Allegory of Evil
source.citation: Spivack, B. (1958). Shakespeare and the Allegory of Evil. Columbia UP (the Vice as the comic tempter-villain of Tudor morality drama).

cards.summary_basic: Before Shakespeare, popular 'morality plays' featured a stock character called the Vice: a gleeful, joking tempter who led the hero into sin and winked at the audience while doing it. Hamlet calls Claudius 'a vice of kings' and 'a king of shreds and patches' — i.e. a cheap, patchwork imitation of a real king, a clownish stage-villain wearing a crown.
cards.detail_scholar: The Vice tradition stands behind several Shakespearean villains who confide in the audience (Richard III, Iago). Here the comparison reduces the smooth, capable Claudius to a tawdry theatrical fraud.

cards.title: The Diet of Worms (a pun)

source.name: Imperial Diet of Worms, 1521
source.citation: The Diet (imperial assembly) held at the German city of Worms in 1521, where Martin Luther was summoned and condemned.

cards.summary_basic: A 'Diet' was a formal assembly of the Holy Roman Empire; the most famous met at the city of Worms in 1521 to try Martin Luther. Hamlet puns on it: Polonius's body is at supper, he says, with 'a certain convocation of politic worms' — an 'assembly of Worms' that are literally eating the corpse. The grim joke folds together church politics, the German city, and grave-worms.
cards.detail_scholar: The pun reinforces the scene's theme that death levels everyone: 'a king may go a progress through the guts of a beggar.' It also fits the play's Wittenberg/Reformation colouring.

cards.title: The antique Roman: honourable suicide

source.name: Plutarch, Lives (North 1579)
source.citation: The Stoic Roman ideal of suicide to avoid dishonour — e.g. Cato the Younger at Utica (46 BCE) and Brutus at Philippi (42 BCE); Plutarch, Lives.

cards.summary_basic: Ancient Roman Stoics admired suicide as a noble, self-possessed response to defeat or dishonour — Cato and Brutus famously killed themselves rather than submit. As Hamlet dies, Horatio grabs the poisoned cup to follow him, declaring 'I am more an antique Roman than a Dane.' Hamlet stops him: Horatio must live to 'tell my story.' The line sets the Roman suicide-ideal against a Christian duty to endure.
cards.detail_scholar: The contrast echoes Hamlet's own earlier wish that God had not 'fix'd his canon 'gainst self-slaughter' — the play repeatedly weighs pagan and Christian attitudes to death.

cards.title: The divine right of kings

source.name: James VI & I, Basilikon Doron
source.citation: James VI & I, The Trew Law of Free Monarchies (1598) and Basilikon Doron (1599): the doctrine that a king is God's anointed deputy, answerable to God alone.

cards.summary_basic: Many in Shakespeare's England believed a king was chosen and protected by God — to harm an anointed monarch was sacrilege. Claudius leans on exactly this when he is threatened: 'There's such divinity doth hedge a king / That treason can but peep to what it would.' The irony is sharp — Claudius himself became king by murdering the rightful one.
cards.detail_scholar: King James I, on the throne soon after Hamlet was written, was the doctrine's loudest champion. The play tests it: the 'divinity' that hedges Claudius is a usurper's shield.

cards.title: Robin Goodfellow

source.name: Scot, The Discoverie of Witchcraft (1584)
source.citation: Reginald Scot, The Discoverie of Witchcraft (1584), Book VII (on hobgoblins, fairies, and Robin Goodfellow).

cards.summary_basic: Robin Goodfellow was an Elizabethan household hobgoblin — a mischievous benign spirit who would do helpful chores overnight (sweep the hearth, grind the malt) in exchange for a bowl of cream, but who would pinch or trip the lazy. Reginald Scot's The Discoverie of Witchcraft (1584) catalogues his pranks — souring the brewer's beer, misleading travellers in the dark, throwing stools — and is the standard source for Puck's self-description in 2.1 of A Midsummer Night's Dream.
cards.detail_scholar: Scot's Discoverie was a sceptical, Reformation-era debunking of witch-belief — so unpopular with the new king that James I tried to suppress it after his accession. Its descriptions of household sprites preserved a folkloric tradition that Shakespeare here turns into the genteel court of Oberon and Titania. Puck's claim to be 'that merry wanderer of the night' draws on the Robin-Goodfellow ballads that circulated in print and oral tradition; the figure also appears in Spenser, Drayton, and Jonson. Puck's name is Old English for goblin or sprite (puca); 'Robin Goodfellow' is the polite, propitiating nickname.

cards.title: The Ides of March

source.name: Plutarch, Life of Caesar; Suetonius, Julius
source.citation: Plutarch, Life of Caesar 63; Suetonius, Julius 81 (Caesar assassinated 15 March 44 BCE).

cards.summary_basic: The Romans named days by counting backward from three fixed points each month: the kalends (the 1st), the nones, and the ides. The ides of March fell on the 15th, the day Julius Caesar was assassinated in 44 BCE.
cards.detail_scholar: A soothsayer warns Caesar, 'Beware the ides of March' (1.2), and on the day itself Caesar taunts him, 'The ides of March are come,' to which the soothsayer replies, 'Ay, Caesar, but not gone' (3.1). Because Romans counted inclusively and backward, dates between the nones and ides were given as so many days 'before the ides.' Plutarch and Suetonius both report the warning and Caesar's dismissal of it; Suetonius adds a crop of omens in the days before the murder.

cards.title: The Feast of Lupercal

source.name: Plutarch, Lives
source.citation: Plutarch, Life of Caesar 61 and Life of Antony 12 (the Lupercalia, mid-February).

cards.summary_basic: The Lupercalia was an ancient Roman fertility festival held in mid-February. Young men ran nearly naked through the city striking bystanders with strips of goatskin; a touch was thought to cure barrenness and ease childbirth.
cards.detail_scholar: The play opens 'on the Lupercal' (1.1); Caesar tells Antony, who is to 'run' the course, 'Forget not in your speed, Antonio, / To touch Calpurnia, for our elders say / The barren, touched in this holy chase, / Shake off their sterile curse' (1.2). At this same festival, Plutarch reports, Antony three times offered Caesar a diadem, which Caesar three times refused while the crowd's reaction made his ambitions plain. Shakespeare compresses Plutarch's account into Casca's sardonic eyewitness report.

cards.title: The Roman Republic and the Name 'King'

source.name: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita; Plutarch, Life of Caesar
source.citation: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 2.1-2; Plutarch, Life of Caesar 60-61 (Republic founded 509 BCE).

cards.summary_basic: Rome had been a republic since it expelled its last king in 509 BCE, and Romans came to loathe one-man rule and the very title 'king' (rex). This is why the thought of crowning Caesar is so explosive in the play.
cards.detail_scholar: Brutus says he loves Caesar but fears the crown: 'How that might change his nature, there's the question' (2.1); Casca reports the people's uneasy response when Caesar is offered the diadem (1.2). After the kings were driven out, Rome was governed by elected magistrates and the Senate, and 'rex' became a hated word; Plutarch stresses that Caesar's apparent reach for kingship, more than his actual power, turned opinion against him. Livy traces the founding of the Republic to the expulsion of the kings.

cards.title: Tarquin and the First Brutus

source.name: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita; Plutarch, Life of Brutus
source.citation: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 1.56-2.1; Plutarch, Life of Brutus 1 (expulsion of the kings, 509 BCE).

cards.summary_basic: Lucius Junius Brutus led the revolt that drove out Rome's last king, Tarquin the Proud, in 509 BCE and founded the Republic. Marcus Brutus, the conspirator in the play, was held to be his descendant, and the plotters use that legacy to draw him in.
cards.detail_scholar: A forged note urges Brutus to live up to his name: 'Shall Rome, etc. Speak, strike, redress! ... My ancestors did from the streets of Rome / The Tarquin drive, when he was call'd a king' (2.1). The first Brutus expelled Tarquin after the rape of Lucretia and, as consul, even condemned his own sons for plotting the king's return; the family thus stood for hatred of monarchy. Cassius and the others exploit this inherited reputation to recruit Marcus Brutus against Caesar.

cards.title: Roman Augury and Omens

source.name: Cicero, De Divinatione; Plutarch, Life of Caesar
source.citation: Cicero, De Divinatione 1; Plutarch, Life of Caesar 63 (the omens before the assassination).

cards.summary_basic: Roman state priests called augurs claimed to read the will of the gods in the flight of birds, in lightning, and in the entrails of sacrificed animals. 'Julius Caesar' is full of such omens warning of disaster.
cards.detail_scholar: Servants report that the priests, sacrificing, 'could not find a heart within the beast' (2.2); the augurers 'would not have him stir to-day' because of this and other portents. Calpurnia's dream and a night of prodigies (a lioness whelping in the streets, graves yielding up their dead) deepen the foreboding. Cicero's 'De Divinatione' is the fullest ancient account of Roman divination; Plutarch records the heartless victim and the augurs' warnings on the eve of Caesar's death.

cards.title: The Proscriptions of the Triumvirate

source.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony; Appian, Civil Wars
source.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 19-21; Appian, Civil Wars 4.5-7 (the proscriptions of 43 BCE).

cards.summary_basic: After Caesar's death, Antony, Octavius, and Lepidus seized power as a triumvirate and posted public lists of citizens to be killed and their property seized. Hundreds of senators and knights died in these proscriptions of 43 BCE, among them the orator Cicero.
cards.detail_scholar: The cold-blooded scene where the three rulers check off names captures this history: 'These many, then, shall die; their names are prick'd. ... your brother too must die; consent you, Lepidus? ... He shall not live; look, with a spot I damn him' (4.1). The men bargain away relatives to settle scores. Plutarch and Appian describe how the triumvirs traded the lives of kinsmen and friends; Cicero, Antony's great enemy, was among the most famous victims.

cards.title: Pompey the Great

source.name: Plutarch, Life of Pompey; Life of Caesar
source.citation: Plutarch, Life of Pompey; Life of Caesar 56-66 (Pharsalus 48 BCE; Munda 45 BCE).

cards.summary_basic: Pompey the Great was Caesar's former ally and son-in-law who became his chief rival. Caesar beat him at Pharsalus in 48 BCE, after which Pompey fled to Egypt and was murdered; his sons fought on until Caesar crushed them at Munda in 45 BCE.
cards.detail_scholar: The tribunes in the first scene are disgusted that the crowd cheers Caesar's triumph over Pompey's sons, recalling how those same Romans once thronged the streets for Pompey himself (1.1). In a grim irony, Caesar is stabbed at the base of Pompey's statue: he 'fell down at the base of Pompey's statue, / Which all the while ran blood' (3.2). Plutarch traces the long rivalry, Pompey's defeat and death in Egypt, and the final war against his sons in Spain.

cards.title: Cato the Younger

source.name: Plutarch, Life of Cato the Younger
source.citation: Plutarch, Life of Cato the Younger (Cato Minor) 66-70 (his suicide at Utica, 46 BCE).

cards.summary_basic: Cato the Younger was a Stoic senator and uncompromising defender of the Republic who killed himself at Utica in 46 BCE rather than live under Caesar. He was the father of Portia and of Young Cato, and the great model of the noble Roman suicide.
cards.detail_scholar: Cato's example shadows the play's deaths. Portia, his daughter, proves her constancy by giving herself 'a voluntary wound' (2.1) and later dies; Brutus invokes his name on the battlefield, where Young Cato is killed crying out his lineage (5.4). Brutus, refusing to be led captive to Rome, dies in the same republican spirit. Plutarch's 'Life of Cato the Younger' gives the famous account of his last night reading Plato's Phaedo before falling on his sword.

cards.title: The Roman Triumph

source.name: Plutarch, Life of Caesar; Roman custom
source.citation: Plutarch, Life of Caesar; Roman triumphal custom (cf. Livy, Ab Urbe Condita).

cards.summary_basic: A triumph was a lavish victory parade voted by the Senate to a Roman general after a major win over a foreign enemy. The honored commander rode through Rome with his army, his spoils, and his captives in a great public procession.
cards.detail_scholar: In the first scene the tribunes Flavius and Murellus rebuke the commoners for making holiday to 'see Caesar and to rejoice in his triumph' (1.1). Their objection is pointed: a triumph was meant to celebrate the conquest of foreign foes, but Caesar's was over the sons of Pompey, fellow Romans, in a civil war. Stripping the statues of their festal decorations, the tribunes try to deflate the cult forming around Caesar.

cards.title: Petrarch and the Petrarchan lover

source.name: Petrarch, Canzoniere
source.citation: Francesco Petrarca (1304-1374), Canzoniere (Rerum vulgarium fragmenta): 366 poems to an idealized 'Laura,' the model for the European love-sonnet.

cards.summary_basic: The Italian poet Petrarch wrote a celebrated sequence of sonnets to an idealized, unattainable woman he called Laura. His imitators across Europe turned it into a whole convention: the cold, chaste mistress, the suffering lover, and a style crammed with contradictions ('freezing fire,' 'sweet pain'). Mercutio teases the lovesick Romeo as a textbook Petrarchan: 'Now is he for the numbers [verses] that Petrarch flow'd in: Laura, to his lady, was but a kitchen-wench' (2.4).
cards.detail_scholar: Romeo's early speeches about Rosaline are pure Petrarchism — 'O brawling love, O loving hate... cold fire, sick health' (1.1) — a heap of oxymorons for a woman who, like Laura, has sworn chastity (see Diana). The play then stages Romeo growing out of this borrowed idiom: his language for Juliet becomes direct, mutual, and sacramental (the shared 'pilgrim' sonnet of 1.5) rather than the one-sided complaint of Petrarchan convention. The 14-line sonnet form itself — which frames the play in its two Choruses and in the lovers' first meeting — is part of Petrarch's legacy.

cards.title: Tybalt, 'Prince of Cats'

source.name: Reynard the Fox (Caxton 1481)
source.citation: The medieval beast-epic Reynard the Fox, whose cat is named Tibert/Tybert; printed in English by William Caxton, 1481. Cf. Thomas Nashe, Have with You to Saffron-Walden (1596), which names 'Tibault ... Prince of Cattes.'

cards.summary_basic: In the old animal fable Reynard the Fox, the cat is named Tibert (or Tybert) — so close to 'Tybalt' that Mercutio puns on it relentlessly, calling Tybalt 'Prince of Cats' and 'good King of Cats' and jeering 'Tybalt, you rat-catcher' (2.4, 3.1). The joke belittles Tybalt's preening, dangerous swordsmanship as merely feline.
cards.detail_scholar: Mercutio spins the gibe into fencing slang: Tybalt fights 'as you sing prick-song,' by the fashionable new Italian rules — 'a duellist, a duellist; a gentleman of the very first house.' Calling Tybalt a cat with nine lives ('Good king of cats, nothing but one of your nine lives,' 3.1) sets up the bitter irony that Mercutio, not Tybalt, is the first to die. Thomas Nashe had already paired the name with the title in print — 'Tibault ... Prince of Cattes' (Have with You to Saffron-Walden, 1596) — so the pun was current with Shakespeare's audience.

cards.title: Queen Mab and the fairies

source.name: Romeo and Juliet 1.4; Elizabethan fairy lore
source.citation: Mercutio's 'Queen Mab' speech, Romeo and Juliet 1.4; cf. Reginald Scot, The Discoverie of Witchcraft (1584) on popular fairy belief.

cards.summary_basic: Queen Mab is the tiny 'fairies' midwife' of Mercutio's famous flight of fancy (1.4): no bigger than the agate-stone on an alderman's ring, she drives a hazelnut chariot over sleepers' faces and makes them dream of what they most desire — lovers of love, lawyers of fees, soldiers of cut throats. The speech turns dreams into wish-fulfilment, then into something dark and disturbing.
cards.detail_scholar: 'Mab' is an English folk-name for the fairy queen; the brilliant elaboration of her is largely Shakespeare's own invention. The speech answers Romeo's belief that his dream is an omen: Mercutio insists dreams are 'the children of an idle brain,' mere vapours — a dismissal that ironically rejects exactly the kind of premonition the tragedy will go on to vindicate. Elizabethan audiences knew a rich tradition of small, mischievous night- and household-spirits (compare Robin Goodfellow).

cards.title: Shrift: the sacrament of confession

source.name: Catholic sacrament of penance
source.citation: Auricular confession to a priest, required at least yearly since the Fourth Lateran Council (1215) and reaffirmed at the Council of Trent (Session 14, 1551); from Old English scrifan, 'to shrive.'

cards.summary_basic: To be 'shrived' (to go to 'shrift') meant to confess one's sins to a priest and receive absolution — a Catholic sacrament. Friar Lawrence is the lovers' 'ghostly [spiritual] father,' their confessor, and the cover for Juliet's secret wedding is that she has gone 'to shrift': 'Hie you to the cell; / There stays a husband to make you a wife' (2.5), while to her family she goes only 'to make confession and to be absolv'd' (4.2).
cards.detail_scholar: The play is set in Catholic Italy, and confession to a friar is the hinge of its secrecy: Juliet can leave home unsupervised because going to shrift is beyond suspicion, and the friar's role as private counsellor lets Lawrence run the whole clandestine plot. In Reformation England the sacrament had been sharply curtailed, so the world of friars, cells, and shriving carried an old-world, foreign, faintly suspect colouring for the first audiences — the same colouring as the disguised friar of Measure for Measure.

cards.title: Pilgrims, palmers, and holy shrines

source.name: Medieval Christian pilgrimage
source.citation: Medieval practice of pilgrimage to saints' shrines (Canterbury, Santiago de Compostela, Jerusalem); a 'palmer' carried a palm frond to show he had reached the Holy Land. Cf. Chaucer, The Canterbury Tales (c. 1387).

cards.summary_basic: Pilgrims travelled to holy shrines to pray at the relics of saints; a 'palmer' was a pilgrim who had reached the Holy Land and carried a palm leaf as proof. When Romeo and Juliet first meet (1.5) they speak an entire shared sonnet built on this image: his lips are 'two blushing pilgrims,' her hand a 'holy shrine,' and a kiss the 'palmers' kiss' — courtship disguised as devotion.
cards.detail_scholar: The conceit is witty and reverent at once: Romeo casts himself as a pilgrim worshipping a saint, and the pun on 'palmer'/'palm' (the flat of the hand) lets the lovers turn pressing palms together into a kind of prayer — 'palm to palm is holy palmers' kiss.' The name 'Romeo' itself meant a pilgrim to Rome in Italian (a romeo), so the saint-and-pilgrim game is quietly built into his name. The fourteen-line sonnet the two jointly compose is the formal sign that this love, unlike his Petrarchan sighing for Rosaline, is mutual and answered.

cards.title: Plague and quarantine

source.name: Bubonic plague in Elizabethan England
source.citation: Recurrent bubonic plague; major London epidemics of 1592-93 and 1603 closed the theatres. Infected houses were sealed and marked, and deaths tallied in the weekly Bills of Mortality.

cards.summary_basic: Plague was a recurring terror in Shakespeare's England; when it struck, the authorities shut up infected houses, marked them, and let no one in or out. This is what dooms the lovers: Friar John, carrying Lawrence's vital letter to Romeo, is sealed by 'the searchers of the town' into a house suspected of 'infectious pestilence' and never delivers it (5.2). Mercutio's dying curse — 'A plague o' both your houses!' (3.1) — names the same dread.
cards.detail_scholar: 'Searchers' were officials, often poor women, who inspected the dead and the sick and reported plague deaths for the Bills of Mortality; a suspected house was sealed, sometimes with a painted cross and the words 'Lord have mercy upon us.' The detail was grimly familiar to audiences whose own playhouses had been closed for months in the 1592-93 outbreak. The whole catastrophe turns on this ordinary public-health measure — a single letter that cannot get through — which is why Friar Lawrence's careful plan miscarries.

cards.title: The shrieking mandrake

source.name: Gerard, The Herball (1597)
source.citation: John Gerard, The Herball, or Generall Historie of Plantes (1597), on mandragora; cf. Pliny, Natural History Book 25 (mandragora as a narcotic plant). The deadly shriek when the root is torn up is medieval folklore, not classical.

cards.summary_basic: The mandrake (mandragora) is a real narcotic plant whose forked root can look eerily like a human body. Folklore held that it grew beneath gallows, that it shrieked when pulled from the earth, and that the shriek killed or maddened whoever heard it. Dreading the tomb, Juliet imagines waking among the dead and hearing 'shrieks like mandrakes torn out of the earth, / That living mortals, hearing them, run mad' (4.3).
cards.detail_scholar: John Gerard's Herball (1597) reports and ridicules the legends — including the tale that a dog must be tied to the root to drag it out, so that the deadly shriek kills the dog instead of the gatherer. The plant's genuine sedative power also lies behind Shakespeare's 'drowsy syrups' and 'mandragora' (Othello 3.3, Antony and Cleopatra 1.5). Juliet's catalogue of tomb-horrors — the mandrake's shriek, the heaped bones, the fresh-bleeding corpse of Tybalt — is one of the play's most vivid evocations of buried-alive panic.

cards.title: Edward III and his seven sons

source.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
source.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland (1587); the descent of the sons of King Edward III (reigned 1327-1377).

cards.summary_basic: Almost every quarrel in Shakespeare's history plays traces back to the children of one king, Edward III, who had seven sons. The lines that matter most are those of his third surviving son, John of Gaunt, Duke of Lancaster (whose son Bolingbroke becomes Henry IV — the house of Lancaster), and his fourth, Edmund of Langley, Duke of York (the house of York). A younger son, Thomas of Woodstock, Duke of Gloucester, has just been murdered as Richard II opens — the grievance behind the play's first scenes. The Duchess of Gloucester sets out the family tree in her 'Edward's seven sons' speech (1.2).
cards.detail_scholar: The rival claims that fuel the Wars of the Roses turn on birth order. Richard II is the son of Edward's eldest son, the Black Prince, and so the rightful king. When Richard dies childless, the senior claim by strict descent runs through Edward's second surviving son, Lionel of Antwerp, Duke of Clarence, whose heiress married into the Mortimer family and thence to the house of York — which is why the Yorkists later argue their title outranks the reigning Lancastrians, who descend from the younger John of Gaunt. Bolingbroke's seizure of the crown in this play is thus the original wound: a younger line displacing the senior, leaving a defect of title that his grandson Henry VI cannot defend. The card recurs wherever a character invokes 'blood,' 'lineal' right, or the Mortimer claim (Henry IV Part 1 1.3 and 3.1; Henry V's Salic-law genealogy; the Temple Garden scene of Henry VI Part 1; and Richard III).

cards.title: The king's two bodies

source.name: Plowden, Commentaries; Kantorowicz
source.citation: Edmund Plowden, Commentaries or Reports (c. 1571), on the body natural and body politic; analysed in E. H. Kantorowicz, The King's Two Bodies (1957), which takes Richard II as its central literary case.

cards.summary_basic: Tudor lawyers held that a king has two bodies in one person: a mortal 'body natural' that ages and dies, and an undying 'body politic' — the office, the crown, the realm itself — which never dies and can do no wrong. Normally the two are inseparable. Richard II dramatizes their violent divorce: when Richard is deposed, the man is pried apart from the office, and he no longer knows what he is — 'I have no name, no title... and know not now what name to call myself' (4.1).
cards.detail_scholar: The doctrine was framed in Plowden's Reports to handle legal puzzles about royal acts and lands; Kantorowicz made Richard II the showpiece of his great study because the deposition scene literally stages the unkinging of the body natural while the body politic passes to Bolingbroke. Richard's obsession with his own name, his shadow, and the mirror (4.1) is the play thinking through what is left of a king once the office is stripped away. The same split underlies Henry IV's careworn 'uneasy lies the head that wears a crown' and Henry V's meditation on 'ceremony' the night before Agincourt.

cards.title: The great chain of being (order and degree)

source.name: Homily Against Disobedience (1571); Tillyard
source.citation: Certain Sermons or Homilies appointed to be read in Churches: 'An Homily Against Disobedience and Wilful Rebellion' (1571); synthesised in E. M. W. Tillyard, The Elizabethan World Picture (1943).

cards.summary_basic: Elizabethans pictured the whole of creation as a fixed ladder or 'chain' of ranks — God above the angels, the angels above the king, the king above his nobles, and so on down through commons, beasts, and plants — each in its appointed 'degree.' To break that order, above all by rebelling against or deposing a king, was thought to loose chaos through nature and the state alike. The fear drives Carlisle's prophecy that deposing Richard will drench England in blood (4.1) and the gardener's allegory of a kingdom gone to weeds (3.4).
cards.detail_scholar: The state preached this doctrine directly: the official Homily Against Disobedience, read aloud in every parish church, taught that rebellion was the worst of sins because it overturned God's ordained order. Shakespeare's most famous dramatic statement of it is Ulysses on 'degree' in Troilus and Cressida ('Take but degree away, untune that string, / And hark what discord follows'). In the histories the principle is what makes usurpation not merely a crime but a cosmic disorder whose consequences echo for generations.

cards.title: The fall of princes (de casibus tragedy)

source.name: Boccaccio; Lydgate; A Mirror for Magistrates
source.citation: Boccaccio, De Casibus Virorum Illustrium (c. 1360); John Lydgate, Fall of Princes (1431-38); A Mirror for Magistrates (1559), which includes a verse tragedy of Richard II.

cards.summary_basic: A 'de casibus' tragedy — Latin for 'concerning the falls' of famous men — tells how the great are cast down from prosperity to ruin by the turning of Fortune, as a warning to the powerful. Richard II is a textbook example: a king toppled from the height of power to a prison grave. Richard knows the tradition and speaks it aloud — 'let us sit upon the ground / And tell sad stories of the death of kings' (3.2).
cards.detail_scholar: The genre runs from Boccaccio through Lydgate's English Fall of Princes to the hugely popular Mirror for Magistrates, an anthology of ghosts of fallen English rulers (Richard II among them) lamenting their downfalls — a direct influence on the history plays. It pairs naturally with the image of Fortune's wheel: the higher the rise, the more spectacular the fall. Shakespeare both uses and complicates the form, giving his fallen princes (Richard II, Henry VI, Wolsey in Henry VIII) an inwardness the bald moral exemplum never had.

cards.title: Trial by combat and the gage

source.name: Medieval law of arms; Holinshed
source.citation: Trial by battle (wager of battle) in medieval English law; Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), records the appeal of treason between Henry Bolingbroke and Thomas Mowbray and the aborted duel at Coventry, 1398.

cards.summary_basic: When one nobleman accused another of treason, the quarrel could be settled by a judicial duel — 'trial by combat' — on the belief that God would grant victory to the side in the right. The accuser threw down a 'gage' (a gauntlet or hood) as a pledge to fight; the accused 'took it up' to accept the challenge. Richard II opens on exactly this ritual: Bolingbroke and Mowbray exchange the lie and their gages (1.1) and meet in the lists at Coventry (1.3) before Richard halts the combat. The gage-throwing erupts again among the lords in 4.1.
cards.detail_scholar: The formal stages are all staged: the appeal of treason, the casting down and taking up of gages, the heralds' proclamations, and the marshalled lists with their throne and warder (the baton Richard throws down to stop the fight). Holinshed describes the historical Coventry duel of September 1398 and Richard's last-moment decision to banish both men rather than let it proceed. The same archaic procedure powers the comic-serious armourer's duel in Henry VI Part 2 (where a master is killed by his own apprentice) and the chivalric challenges of the later histories.

cards.title: Holinshed's Chronicles

source.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
source.citation: Raphael Holinshed et al., The Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland, 2nd edition (1587) — Shakespeare's principal source for the English history plays, and for Macbeth, King Lear, and Cymbeline.

cards.summary_basic: Holinshed's Chronicles was the great Tudor history book that Shakespeare mined for nearly all of his English history plays. For Richard II it supplied the events of 1398-1400: the quarrel and double banishment of Bolingbroke and Mowbray, John of Gaunt's death and Richard's seizure of his estate, Bolingbroke's return from exile, the deposition, and Richard's murder at Pomfret.
cards.detail_scholar: First published in 1577 and expanded in the 1587 second edition (the one Shakespeare used), the Chronicles were a collaborative compilation. Shakespeare follows their narrative closely but compresses time, invents private scenes, and sharpens motive; for Richard II he also drew on Samuel Daniel's verse history The Civil Wars (1595) and probably on Froissart. The same volume is the quarry for the whole second tetralogy, the Henry VI plays and Richard III, and — outside the histories — for Macbeth, King Lear, and Cymbeline.

cards.title: Gad's Hill and highway robbery

source.name: The Famous Victories of Henry the Fifth (c. 1586)
source.citation: The Famous Victories of Henry the Fifth (anon., c. 1586), which also stages a Gad's Hill robbery; Gad's Hill is a rise on the old London-Dover road near Rochester, Kent, proverbial for highwaymen.

cards.summary_basic: Gad's Hill, a steep rise on the main road from London to Dover near Rochester in Kent, was notorious in Shakespeare's day as a lair of highwaymen who preyed on travellers and pilgrims bound for Canterbury. The play stages a robbery there: Falstaff's gang waylay travellers carrying money toward the court (2.2), only to be robbed in turn by the disguised Hal and Poins. One of the thieves is even named Gadshill after the place.
cards.detail_scholar: The same robbery episode appears in Shakespeare's source play, The Famous Victories of Henry the Fifth, fixing the location's place in the Hal legend. The Chamberlain's tip about a wealthy franklin carrying 'three hundred marks' and 'pilgrims going to Canterbury with rich offerings' (2.1) reflects the real traffic of the Dover road. The robbers' cant — 'minions of the moon,' 'Saint Nicholas' clerks' for thieves — belongs to a whole Elizabethan rogue literature.

cards.title: The Battle of Shrewsbury (1403)

source.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
source.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the Battle of Shrewsbury, 21 July 1403, where Henry IV defeated the Percy rebellion and Hotspur was slain.

cards.summary_basic: The Battle of Shrewsbury (21 July 1403) was the real clash in which Henry IV crushed the Percy rebellion. Hotspur was killed and his army broken, and his uncle Worcester was captured and executed soon after. Shakespeare makes the battle the play's climax and, for dramatic effect, has Prince Hal kill Hotspur in single combat.
cards.detail_scholar: Hal's killing of Hotspur is a heroic invention: the chronicles do not credit the prince with the kill, and the real Hal, about sixteen, was himself wounded in the face by an arrow at Shrewsbury. Shakespeare also compresses chronology (Hotspur was in fact a generation older than the prince) to set the two young men as foils. The detail of nobles 'marching in the King's coats' as decoys, and Douglas cutting them down one by one, comes from Holinshed.

cards.title: Falstaff and Sir John Oldcastle

source.name: The Famous Victories; Foxe, Acts and Monuments (1563)
source.citation: Sir John Oldcastle, Lord Cobham, Lollard knight burned for heresy and treason in 1417; named as the prince's companion in The Famous Victories of Henry the Fifth (anon., c. 1586); honoured as a martyr in John Foxe, Acts and Monuments (1563).

cards.summary_basic: Falstaff was first written under the name Sir John Oldcastle — the name the fat knight bears in Shakespeare's source play. The real Oldcastle was a Lollard (proto-Protestant) knight and friend of the historical Prince Hal, later burned as a heretic and traitor in 1417 and revered by Elizabethan Protestants as a martyr. His powerful descendants objected to seeing their ancestor played as a coward and glutton, and Shakespeare changed the name to Falstaff. The Epilogue's promise that 'Oldcastle died a martyr, and this is not the man' is a public disclaimer of the link.
cards.detail_scholar: A trace of the original name survives in Henry IV Part 1, where Hal calls Falstaff 'my old lad of the castle' (1.2). After the Cobham family's protest the name was changed across the plays, and a rival company answered with its own admiring play, Sir John Oldcastle (1599), whose prologue insists their hero was 'no pampered glutton.' Foxe's hugely influential Acts and Monuments ('Foxe's Book of Martyrs') had enshrined Oldcastle as a Protestant hero — which is exactly why turning him into a comic reprobate was provocative, and why the Henry IV Part 2 Epilogue takes such pains to separate the two.

cards.title: The Jerusalem Chamber and the prophecy

source.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
source.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the death of Henry IV in the Jerusalem Chamber of Westminster Abbey, 20 March 1413, and the prophecy that he should die in Jerusalem.

cards.summary_basic: Henry IV had been told by a prophecy that he would die in Jerusalem, and took it to mean he would die on crusade in the Holy Land — a journey he longs for across both parts of the play. Instead he collapses and is carried to a room in Westminster Abbey that happens to be named the Jerusalem Chamber. Learning its name, he accepts the grim joke of the prophecy: 'In that Jerusalem shall Harry die' (4.5). The historical Henry IV did die there on 20 March 1413.
cards.detail_scholar: The episode comes straight from Holinshed, who reports the prophecy and the King's recognition of its fulfilment. It caps the play's running ache of the crusade Henry vowed but never made — first raised in the opening lines of Part 1 ('to chase these pagans in those holy fields') and revived here as he dies. The irony is characteristic of the play's bleak view of power: even the King's penitential dream of Jerusalem is granted only as a deathbed pun.

cards.title: Prince Hal and the Lord Chief Justice

source.name: Elyot, The Boke Named the Governour (1531)
source.citation: Sir Thomas Elyot, The Boke Named the Governour (1531), Book II, on Prince Hal striking the Lord Chief Justice (traditionally Sir William Gascoigne) and being committed to prison; repeated in Hall and Holinshed.

cards.summary_basic: A famous story, told by the Tudor moralist Sir Thomas Elyot, held that the wild Prince Hal once struck the Lord Chief Justice in open court — and that the judge boldly committed the prince to prison for contempt, which Hal, coming to his senses, accepted. The episode lies behind the tense relationship in this play: the Chief Justice fears the new King's revenge, but Henry V instead praises his courage, confirms him in office, and bids him be 'a father to my youth' (5.2).
cards.detail_scholar: Elyot's Governour offered the anecdote as a model of both a just magistrate who would not bend the law for a prince and a prince wise enough to honour the rebuke. Shakespeare dramatizes the reconciliation as the keystone of Hal's transformation from tavern-rogue to lawful king: where the rejection of Falstaff shows what the new King casts off, the embrace of the Chief Justice shows what he takes up — impartial public justice over private favour. The judge is traditionally identified with Sir William Gascoigne, though the historical particulars are uncertain.

cards.title: The Salic law and Henry's claim to France

source.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
source.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), reproducing Archbishop Chichele's parliamentary argument on the Salic law: 'In terram Salicam mulieres ne succedant' (into Salic land let not women succeed).

cards.summary_basic: Henry V's war on France turns on a disputed point of inheritance law. The French invoked the 'Salic law' — 'In terram Salicam mulieres ne succedant,' that no woman may inherit Salic land — to bar Henry's claim, which ran through a female line (his great-great-grandmother Isabella of France). In 1.2 the Archbishop of Canterbury demolishes the objection in a long, dizzying genealogical speech, arguing the Salic land lay in Germany, not France, and that French kings had themselves inherited through women. He pronounces the claim good, and the King goes to war.
cards.detail_scholar: Shakespeare takes Canterbury's speech almost verbatim from Holinshed (who reproduces Archbishop Chichele's argument), tangled genealogy and all. The scene is deliberately double-edged: the justification is both solemnly important — it is the play's casus belli, and Henry insists the Church answer for it 'on your head' — and, in its impenetrable detail, faintly absurd, leaving open the question whether the war is just or merely well-lawyered. The underlying descent is the same Edward III genealogy that drives the dynastic quarrels of all the histories.

cards.title: The Battle of Agincourt (1415)

source.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
source.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the Battle of Agincourt, 25 October 1415: the English longbowmen, the miry field, the lopsided casualties, and the killing of the prisoners.

cards.summary_basic: Agincourt (25 October 1415) was Henry V's astonishing victory over a far larger French army and the climax of the play. A small, sick, exhausted English force — its strength in the longbowmen — destroyed the flower of French chivalry, bogged in mud and packed too tight to fight. Shakespeare keeps the chronicles' lopsided count: thousands of French dead against a handful of English. The play stages the eve of battle, the St. Crispin's Day speech, and the controversial order to kill the French prisoners.
cards.detail_scholar: Holinshed supplies the heavily outnumbered English (Shakespeare preserves the disproportion for its glory), the rain-soaked field that mired the heavy French cavalry, and the order to kill the prisoners — which the play motivates twice over, by a renewed French attack and by the French raid on the boys guarding the baggage (4.7). Contemporaries read the near-miraculous result as a sign of divine favour, and Henry forbids any man to boast of it on pain of death, giving God the glory ('O God, thy arm was here'). The longbow's dominance over armoured knights marks a turning point in medieval warfare.

cards.title: Saint Crispin's Day

source.name: Jacobus de Voragine, The Golden Legend (c. 1260)
source.citation: Feast of Saints Crispin and Crispinian, 25 October; the martyred shoemaker brothers of the third century (Jacobus de Voragine, The Golden Legend, c. 1260). Agincourt was fought on their feast day in 1415.

cards.summary_basic: Agincourt was fought on 25 October, the feast day of Saints Crispin and Crispinian — two early Christian brothers, patron saints of shoemakers, martyred in the third century. Henry seizes on the coincidence in the speech rallying his outnumbered men: those who survive will remember the date forever and each year 'strip his sleeve and show his scars,' while 'we few, we happy few, we band of brothers' will be honoured to the ending of the world (4.3).
cards.detail_scholar: The legend of the cobbler-saints comes from the medieval Golden Legend; their feast gave the battle its enduring English name. Shakespeare's speech transforms a saints' day into a secular cult of memory and male fellowship — the soldiers' shared danger levels rank ('be he ne'er so vile, / This day shall gentle his condition'), and the reward held out is not heaven but everlasting fame. It is the most quoted of all the play's set-pieces.

cards.title: The Southampton plot

source.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
source.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the conspiracy of Richard, Earl of Cambridge, Henry, Lord Scroop of Masham, and Sir Thomas Grey, exposed at Southampton, August 1415.

cards.summary_basic: On the eve of sailing for France, Henry uncovers a plot to murder him at Southampton, hatched by three trusted men — the Earl of Cambridge, Lord Scroop, and Sir Thomas Grey, bribed (the play says) with French gold. Henry traps them into urging severity for a minor offender, then confronts them with their own treason and sends them to execution (2.2). He is wounded above all by Scroop, his intimate friend, whose betrayal he calls 'like / Another fall of man.'
cards.detail_scholar: The historical conspiracy had a dynastic edge the play half-buries: Cambridge's real aim, as Holinshed hints and the later Henry VI plays make explicit, was to set his brother-in-law Edmund Mortimer — the Yorkist claimant by the senior Edward III line — on the throne. Shakespeare reduces the motive to French money to keep Henry's cause untainted, though Cambridge's cryptic confession that he was moved by something besides gold gestures at the deeper claim. The episode shows the new King's cold, providential justice — and the lurking flaw in the Lancastrian title that will reopen after his death.

cards.title: The 'wooden O' and the Chorus's apology

source.name: The Elizabethan public playhouse; the Globe (1599)
source.citation: The open-air amphitheatre playhouses of London (the Curtain; the Globe, built 1599, the likely first home of Henry V); the Chorus's 'this wooden O' (Prologue).

cards.summary_basic: Henry V is unique among Shakespeare's plays in giving a Chorus an apology before every act for the theatre's limits, begging the audience to supply the rest with imagination. He calls the round playhouse a 'wooden O' and a 'cockpit,' too small to hold 'the vasty fields of France,' and asks the audience to 'piece out our imperfections with your thoughts' — to 'think, when we talk of horses, that you see them.' It is Shakespeare's most sustained meditation on how theatre works.
cards.detail_scholar: The 'wooden O' is the circular, open-roofed public amphitheatre — most likely the newly built Globe (1599) or possibly the Curtain. The Chorus's repeated apologies are partly conventional modesty and partly a real problem: how to stage Agincourt, a Channel crossing, and two kingdoms on a bare platform. By turning that limitation into the play's theme, Shakespeare makes the audience's imagination a collaborator — and quietly flatters it. The device also lets him leap over years and miles between acts and frame the warrior-king as a figure of epic report.

cards.title: Crécy, Poitiers, and the Black Prince

source.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
source.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Edward III's victory at Crécy (1346) and his son Edward the Black Prince's victory at Poitiers (1356) in the Hundred Years' War.

cards.summary_basic: When the French king weighs the English threat, he remembers two catastrophic French defeats of the previous century: Crécy (1346), won by Edward III, and Poitiers (1356), won by his son Edward the Black Prince, who captured the French king himself. Henry V consciously claims that heritage — Canterbury urges him to 'forage in the blood' of his warlike ancestors (1.2), and the French dread that 'this is a stem / Of that victorious stock' (2.4). The old battles are the precedent that makes Agincourt thinkable.
cards.detail_scholar: Crécy and Poitiers were the showpiece English victories of the first phase of the Hundred Years' War, both won — as Agincourt would be — by the longbow against a numerically superior, more heavily armoured French force. The Black Prince (so called from his armour) became the model of the warrior-heir, an obvious template for Shakespeare's Henry; his capture of King John II at Poitiers haunts the French court's fear in 2.4. The card connects to the larger Edward III genealogy that both legitimates Henry's claim and seeds the later dynastic wars.

cards.title: The Wars of the Roses

source.name: Edward Hall, The Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families of Lancaster and York (1548); Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
source.citation: The dynastic civil wars c. 1455-1487 between the houses of Lancaster (red rose) and York (white rose); the rose badges and the Temple-garden quarrel are dramatized in 1 Henry VI 2.4. The collective name 'Wars of the Roses' was popularized much later (Sir Walter Scott, 1829).

cards.summary_basic: The Wars of the Roses were the civil wars (roughly 1455-1487) for the English crown between two branches of the royal family: the house of Lancaster, whose badge was a red rose, and the house of York, whose badge was a white rose. Both descended from King Edward III, so both could claim the throne. Shakespeare gives the feud a memorable origin in 1 Henry VI: in the Temple garden the lords pluck red or white roses to declare their sides, and Warwick foresees that the quarrel 'shall send... a thousand souls to death and deadly night.'
cards.detail_scholar: The white rose was a genuine Yorkist badge; the red rose of Lancaster was less used at the time and was promoted afterward, above all by the Tudors, whose 'Tudor rose' fused red and white to symbolize the union of the houses through Henry VII's marriage to Elizabeth of York (1486) — the reconciliation toward which Shakespeare's whole first tetralogy points. The Temple-garden rose-plucking (2.4) is Shakespeare's invention, a piece of symbolic stagecraft dramatizing a division that historically hardened over decades. The underlying cause is genealogical: Lancaster ruled by descent from Edward III's third surviving son, John of Gaunt, while York claimed a senior right through the line of the second son, Lionel of Clarence.

cards.title: Joan la Pucelle (Joan of Arc)

source.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587); the records of Joan's 1431 trial
source.citation: Jeanne d'Arc, c. 1412-1431; 'la Pucelle' = 'the Maid.' Helped raise the siege of Orleans (1429) and saw Charles VII crowned at Reims; captured, tried, and burned by the English at Rouen (30 May 1431). Conviction annulled 1456; canonized a saint in 1920.

cards.summary_basic: Joan la Pucelle — 'the Maid,' known to history as Joan of Arc — was a French peasant girl who said visions of saints had sent her to drive the English out of France. She helped raise the siege of Orleans in 1429 and had the Dauphin crowned king, then was captured, condemned as a heretic and witch, and burned at the stake by the English in 1431. Shakespeare, writing for an English audience, portrays her with hostility — brave at first, then a sorceress who traffics with fiends and lies to escape the fire.
cards.detail_scholar: Shakespeare's deeply unsympathetic Joan reflects English and Tudor-Protestant attitudes (and Holinshed's hostile account), not the historical record or the French and Catholic view; the Church annulled her conviction in 1456 and canonized her in 1920. In the play she is by turns a divinely-inspired warrior ('Astraea's daughter'), a coarse camp-follower, and finally a witch deserted by her familiar spirits who denies her own father and pleads a false pregnancy to delay execution — a portrait that drains away the heroism the early scenes grant her. Some scholars assign the most scurrilous scenes to a collaborator. Her opposition to the chivalric Talbot is the play's central contrast.

cards.title: John Talbot, Earl of Shrewsbury

source.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587); Hall, Union (1548)
source.citation: John Talbot, 1st Earl of Shrewsbury, c. 1387-1453; the leading English commander of the last phase of the Hundred Years' War, killed with his son at the battle of Castillon (1453) — the play's 'Bordeaux.'

cards.summary_basic: Lord Talbot was the foremost English soldier of the later Hundred Years' War — so feared by the French that Shakespeare calls him 'the terror of the French' and has mothers still their children with his name. The play makes him the embodiment of old-fashioned English chivalry and courage, set against both the French and the self-serving nobles at home. When the rival dukes York and Somerset refuse, out of spite, to send the cavalry he needs, he and his son John are surrounded and killed — a death the play blames squarely on the feud tearing England apart.
cards.detail_scholar: The historical Talbot died at Castillon in 1453, the battle that effectively ended the Hundred Years' War; Shakespeare compresses and relocates events but keeps the essential pathos. The death scene of father and son (4.5-4.7) was singled out by Thomas Nashe in 1592 (Pierce Penniless) as moving 'ten thousand spectators at least (at several times)' to tears — rare contemporary evidence of an Elizabethan audience's response to a Shakespeare play, and the strongest external clue to 1 Henry VI's early popularity. Talbot is the play's tragic center: his chivalric heroism is rendered obsolete and finally destroyed by the new politics of faction embodied in the rose quarrel.

cards.title: The Siege of Orleans

source.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
source.citation: The English siege of Orleans, October 1428 - May 1429; relieved by a French army inspired by Joan of Arc — the turning point of the Hundred Years' War. The Earl of Salisbury was killed by a cannon shot early in the siege.

cards.summary_basic: Orleans was a key French city the English besieged in 1428-29. Its relief — credited to Joan of Arc — was the turning point of the Hundred Years' War, after which the tide ran against England. Much of the first two acts of 1 Henry VI dramatizes the siege: the cannon shot that kills the Earl of Salisbury on the walls, Talbot's single combat with Joan, and the loss and night-time recapture of the town. Shakespeare freely rearranges the history for dramatic effect.
cards.detail_scholar: Historically the English had nearly starved Orleans into surrender when Joan arrived; her relief of the city in May 1429 broke the siege and led within months to Charles VII's coronation at Reims. Shakespeare telescopes and reorders events: Salisbury's death by cannon-fire (1.4) is historical, but the play's seesaw sequence of losses and recaptures is shaped for the stage, alternating French and English fortunes to dramatize the war's reversals and to stage a Talbot-Joan rivalry that history did not provide.

cards.title: The Order of the Garter

source.name: Founded by Edward III, c. 1348
source.citation: England's highest order of chivalry; motto 'Honi soit qui mal y pense' ('Shamed be he who thinks evil of it'). In 1 Henry VI 4.1 Talbot tears the Garter from the leg of the cowardly Sir John Fastolfe.

cards.summary_basic: The Order of the Garter, founded by Edward III around 1348, was England's highest order of knighthood — its members the flower of chivalry, sworn to courage and honor. In 1 Henry VI 4.1 Talbot publicly tears the Garter from the leg of Sir John Fastolfe, who fled in battle, and recites what the emblem is meant to stand for: a knight should be 'valiant and... full of haughty courage,' and one who runs from the enemy 'profanes this most honourable order.' The scene measures the play's true chivalry (Talbot) against its decay.
cards.detail_scholar: The Garter's motto and its founding by Edward III tie it to the same heroic past the play mourns. Talbot's stripping of Fastolfe stages the gap between the chivalric ideal and the self-interested reality of England's commanders, and belongs to the play's larger contrast between old-style honor and the new politics of faction. (The cowardly Sir John Fastolfe of this play is distinct from the fat comic knight Falstaff of the Henry IV plays, though the names have often been confused; Shakespeare himself renamed his comic knight after early objections.)

cards.title: Jack Cade's Rebellion

source.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587); Hall, Union (1548)
source.citation: The Kentish revolt of 1450 led by Jack Cade, who took the name 'John Mortimer' and briefly held London. Shakespeare blends it with details of the 1381 Peasants' Revolt (Wat Tyler, Jack Straw) for a broader picture of popular insurrection.

cards.summary_basic: Jack Cade led a real rebellion of Kentish commoners against Henry VI's government in 1450; his men briefly seized London before the rising collapsed. In 2 Henry VI (Act 4) Shakespeare turns Cade into a grotesque comic demagogue — secretly egged on by the Duke of York — who promises cheap food and common ownership, declares 'all the realm shall be in common,' and has his followers hang the Clerk of Chartham for the crime of being able to read and write. The episode stages the chaos that follows when lawful order breaks down.
cards.detail_scholar: Shakespeare conflates the 1450 revolt with memories of the 1381 Peasants' Revolt (Wat Tyler and Jack Straw, the burning of the Savoy, the killing of lawyers and the destruction of records), producing a composite image of mob rule that reflects Tudor anxieties about the 'many-headed multitude' and the period's recurrent food riots. Dick the Butcher's 'The first thing we do, let's kill all the lawyers' is the play's most-quoted line; in context it is the rebels' fantasy of erasing the written law that binds and records them. York's secret sponsorship (3.1) makes the rising a cynical test of how far the commons will follow a claimant to the crown.

cards.title: Eleanor Cobham and the Witchcraft Trial

source.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587); Hall, Union (1548)
source.citation: Eleanor Cobham, Duchess of Gloucester, convicted in 1441 of treasonable necromancy for procuring the casting of the King's horoscope with the priest Roger Bolingbroke and the 'Witch of Eye,' Margery Jourdain; she did public penance and was imprisoned for life.

cards.summary_basic: In 1441 Eleanor Cobham, wife of the Lord Protector the Duke of Gloucester, was convicted of treasonable witchcraft: she had employed a priest, a conjurer, and a 'cunning woman' to foretell — and perhaps hasten — the death of the young King Henry VI. To foresee the monarch's death was treason. She did public penance, walking through London in a sheet, and was imprisoned for life; the scandal helped bring down her husband. 2 Henry VI dramatizes the conjuring (1.4), the arrest, and the penance (2.3-2.4).
cards.detail_scholar: Predicting a reigning monarch's death by astrology or magic counted as treason because the prophecy could become an incitement; the anxiety was still live in Shakespeare's day, when casting the Queen's horoscope was a serious crime and Parliament passed witchcraft statutes (1563, strengthened 1604). The conjured spirit answers in equivocating prophecies — the King shall be deposed by one who 'shall depose,' the Duke of Suffolk shall die 'by water,' Somerset should 'shun castles' — riddles whose ironic fulfilment the play then stages. Margery Jourdain (the 'Witch of Eye') and Roger Bolingbroke were real people executed for the conspiracy; the conjurer shares a surname with, but is unrelated to, the usurping Henry Bolingbroke of Richard II.

cards.title: Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester ('Good Duke Humphrey')

source.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587); Hall, Union (1548)
source.citation: Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester (1390-1447), youngest son of Henry IV and Lord Protector during Henry VI's minority; a noted patron of learning. He died suddenly under arrest at Bury St Edmunds in 1447, widely rumored to have been murdered.

cards.summary_basic: Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester, was the young King Henry VI's uncle and Lord Protector — popularly called 'good Duke Humphrey' for his reputation as an honest defender of the commonwealth. In 2 Henry VI he is the realm's moral anchor, hated by the queen's faction for his integrity and his power. His enemies engineer his wife's disgrace, strip him of office, arrest him on empty charges of treason, and have him murdered — a death the play presents as the moment England loses its last protector against ruin.
cards.detail_scholar: The historical Humphrey was a genuine patron of humanist learning whose book collection became the foundation of 'Duke Humfrey's Library' at Oxford (later absorbed into the Bodleian). He died in custody at Bury St Edmunds in 1447; whether by murder or natural causes is unknown, but contemporary rumor and Tudor chronicle treated it as foul play, and Shakespeare stages a strangling that Warwick exposes from the marks on the corpse (3.2). His fall removes the last restraint on the ambition of Suffolk, Margaret, the Cardinal, and York, and clears the path to civil war.

cards.title: The First Battle of St Albans

source.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
source.citation: 22 May 1455, usually reckoned the opening battle of the Wars of the Roses; the Duke of York and the Nevilles defeated the royal army at St Albans, killing the Duke of Somerset and Lord Clifford. Dramatized at the close of 2 Henry VI (Act 5).

cards.summary_basic: The first battle of St Albans (1455) is usually counted the opening battle of the Wars of the Roses, and it ends 2 Henry VI. The Duke of York, having dropped the pretense of merely wanting Somerset removed, defeats the King's forces; his son Richard kills Somerset, and York kills old Lord Clifford. The discovery of his father's body turns the young Clifford into the merciless avenger who haunts the next play, as the dynastic war the rose-quarrel predicted finally breaks into open slaughter.
cards.detail_scholar: Historically a short, sharp fight in the streets of the town rather than a pitched battle, St Albans gave the Yorkists custody of the King and removed their chief rival, Somerset. Shakespeare uses it to pay off two prophecies from the conjuring scene (1.4): Somerset dies 'by a castle' (beneath the sign of the Castle alehouse), and Young Clifford's vow of revenge ('York not our old men spares; no more will I their babes') sets the tone of escalating atrocity for 3 Henry VI.

cards.title: The Battle of Towton

source.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587); Hall, Union (1548)
source.citation: 29 March 1461 (Palm Sunday), fought in a snowstorm near Towton, Yorkshire; reckoned the largest and bloodiest battle on English soil, a decisive Yorkist victory that secured the throne for the newly proclaimed Edward IV. Dramatized across 3 Henry VI Act 2.

cards.summary_basic: Towton (1461) was the bloodiest battle ever fought on English soil — a day-long slaughter in a snowstorm that confirmed the young Edward IV as king and shattered the Lancastrian army. Shakespeare dramatizes it across the middle of 3 Henry VI: Warwick swears to fight on foot to the death, Richard hunts Clifford, and — most memorably — the helpless King Henry sits on a molehill and watches a son who has unknowingly killed his father and a father who has killed his son, the play's central image of civil war's horror.
cards.detail_scholar: Contemporary chronicles put the dead in the tens of thousands (probably exaggerated, though the carnage was real — a mass grave was excavated near the site in 1996). Shakespeare uses the battle less for military detail than for its emblematic 'molehill' scene (2.5): against the usual de casibus convention of the fall of the mighty, here the suffering is the common soldier's and the realm's, and the king — who ought to govern the storm — can only lament it and wish himself a simple shepherd. The interlude crystallizes the trilogy's vision of a kingdom devouring itself, answering York's own molehill humiliation at Wakefield (1.4) and marking the moral nadir from which only the distant Tudor settlement will recover.

cards.title: The Stage Machiavel

source.name: Niccolo Machiavelli, The Prince (Il Principe, written 1513, printed 1532); Innocent Gentillet, Contre-Machiavel (1576, English translation 1602)
source.citation: The Elizabethan stage villain built on a lurid caricature of Machiavelli — the amoral schemer who uses fraud, cruelty, and hypocrisy to seize power. Richard names him directly in 3 Henry VI 3.2: he will 'set the murderous Machiavel to school.' Compare the prologue-speaker 'Machevill' in Marlowe's The Jew of Malta (c. 1590).

cards.summary_basic: The 'Machiavel' was a stock villain of the Elizabethan stage: a cold, clever schemer who holds that the end justifies any means and who delights in deceit, betrayal, and murder. He took his name from the Italian writer Niccolo Machiavelli, whose book The Prince was read in England as a handbook for tyranny. Richard of Gloucester is the supreme English example — he boasts in 3 Henry VI that he could 'set the murderous Machiavel to school,' that is, teach the master himself. Like all such villains, he relishes his own wickedness and confides his plots to the audience in soliloquy.
cards.detail_scholar: Few Elizabethans read Machiavelli at first hand; the popular bogeyman came largely through Innocent Gentillet's hostile Contre-Machiavel (1576; English 1602) and through the theatre, where 'Machiavel' became shorthand for atheistic cunning — Marlowe's Jew of Malta is introduced by a character called 'Machevill.' The type fuses with the older native morality-play Vice (see the-vice): Richard explicitly likens himself to 'the formal Vice, Iniquity' (Richard III 3.1). Both traditions give the villain a gleeful, confiding intimacy with the audience, which is why Richard's soliloquies are so seductive even as they horrify. Iago, Edmund, and Aaron the Moor are later variations on the same Machiavellian figure.

cards.title: More's History of King Richard III

source.name: Sir Thomas More, The History of King Richard III (written c. 1513-1518; printed 1557)
source.citation: More's unfinished account of Richard's usurpation — the source, transmitted through Edward Hall (1548) and Holinshed (1587), of the 'crookbacked tyrant' Shakespeare inherited, including the murder of the princes, the council-scene theatre, and Richard's hypocritical piety.

cards.summary_basic: Most of what Shakespeare's audience 'knew' about Richard III came from one book: Sir Thomas More's History of King Richard III, written about 1513. More — later famous as the martyr of his clash with Henry VIII — painted Richard as a deformed, dissembling murderer who killed his way to the throne, and supplied vivid set-pieces (the strawberries at the council, the show of 'refusing' the crown, the smothering of the princes) that Shakespeare dramatizes almost directly. Through the chroniclers Hall and Holinshed, More's portrait fixed Richard as history's archetypal villain.
cards.detail_scholar: More wrote under Henry VIII, when blackening the last Yorkist king flattered the ruling Tudors, and he likely drew on the memories of Cardinal Morton (the Bishop of Ely of the play), Richard's enemy — so the History is brilliant literature and Tudor partisanship rather than neutral record. It is nonetheless the wellspring of the stage Richard: the council-scene theatre (3.4-3.7), the 'two bishops' charade, the ironies of Richard's mock-reluctance, and Tyrrell's smothering of the princes all descend from More by way of Hall and Holinshed. Modern revisionists (and the Richard III Society) contest the portrait, and the 2012 discovery of Richard's scoliotic skeleton showed the 'crookback' was magnified from a real but lesser deformity. The card matters because it explains why the play's Richard is so theatrically self-aware: More had already made him a consummate actor.

cards.title: The Princes in the Tower

source.name: Sir Thomas More, The History of King Richard III (c. 1513-18); Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
source.citation: Edward V (b. 1470) and his brother Richard, Duke of York (b. 1473), sons of Edward IV; lodged in the Tower of London by their uncle Richard of Gloucester in 1483 and never seen again. More's account names Sir James Tyrrell as the agent of their smothering. Two children's skeletons found in the Tower in 1674 were reinterred in Westminster Abbey.

cards.summary_basic: After Edward IV died in 1483, his two young sons — twelve-year-old Edward V and his little brother Richard — were placed in the Tower of London by their uncle, Richard of Gloucester, supposedly for safekeeping before the coronation. Richard had the boys declared illegitimate, took the crown himself as Richard III, and the princes were never seen again. They are believed to have been murdered on his orders. Their fate — innocent children destroyed for a crown — became the defining horror of his reign and the crime that turns the play decisively against him.
cards.detail_scholar: The disappearance of the princes is one of history's famous unsolved cases. Shakespeare follows Thomas More's hostile account (via Hall and Holinshed), in which Sir James Tyrrell arranges the smothering of the sleeping boys by Miles Forrest and John Dighton — the version reported in 4.3. Modern historians debate Richard's guilt and note rival suspects (the Duke of Buckingham, or even Henry VII later), but for Shakespeare the murder is certain and pivotal: it is the act that curdles Richard's support, drives Buckingham to revolt, and seals his damnation. In 1674 workmen in the Tower found a chest of children's bones, which Charles II had reinterred in Westminster Abbey as the princes' remains.

cards.title: The Battle of Bosworth Field

source.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587); Polydore Vergil, Anglica Historia (1534)
source.citation: 22 August 1485, Leicestershire; Henry Tudor, Earl of Richmond, defeated and killed Richard III, partly through the Stanleys' defection. Richard was the last English king to die in battle and the last Plantagenet; Richmond was crowned Henry VII. (Richard's remains were rediscovered in Leicester in 2012.)

cards.summary_basic: Bosworth Field (1485) was the battle that ended both Richard III's reign and the Wars of the Roses. Henry Tudor, Earl of Richmond, landed from exile with a small army; at the decisive moment Lord Stanley's forces, which Richard had counted on, held back. Richard, refusing to flee, was cut down fighting — the last English king to die in battle. The play stages his desperate cry, 'A horse! a horse! my kingdom for a horse!' and his death, after which Richmond is crowned and pledges to unite the warring houses as King Henry VII.
cards.detail_scholar: Shakespeare compresses the campaign into a single climactic night and day (5.2-5.5) and frames it as a providential judgment: the ghosts of Richard's victims bless Richmond and curse Richard, and Richmond's closing speech ('Now civil wounds are stopp'd, peace lives again') proclaims the Tudor settlement. The treachery of the Stanleys was real and decisive; Lord Stanley (Richmond's stepfather) withheld his men although his son was Richard's hostage. By tradition the crown was found on the field and set on Henry's head. In 2012 Richard's skeleton — its spine curved by scoliosis, lending a grain of truth to the 'crookback' image — was excavated from the former Grey Friars church in Leicester and reburied in 2015.

cards.title: Richmond and the Tudor Myth

source.name: Edward Hall, The Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families of Lancaster and York (1548); Polydore Vergil; Thomas More
source.citation: Henry Tudor (1457-1509), Earl of Richmond, who became Henry VII after Bosworth (1485) and married Elizabeth of York (January 1486), uniting the two houses. The 'Tudor myth' is the providential reading of this history — civil war as divine punishment, the Tudors as Heaven-sent restorers — that shaped Hall, Holinshed, and Shakespeare's history plays.

cards.summary_basic: Richmond — Henry Tudor — is the figure through whom the bloody cycle of the history plays finally heals. By defeating Richard at Bosworth and then marrying Elizabeth of York, he joined the rival houses of Lancaster and York in the 'Tudor rose' and founded the dynasty that ruled England in Shakespeare's own day (Queen Elizabeth I was his granddaughter). The Tudor chroniclers read the long wars as God's punishment for the deposition of Richard II, with Henry VII as the providential deliverer — which is why Shakespeare's Richmond speaks less like an ordinary man than like an instrument of Heaven.
cards.detail_scholar: The 'Tudor myth' (a modern label, associated with E. M. W. Tillyard but rooted in Hall's 1548 Union and in More and Polydore Vergil) frames the whole stretch from Richard II to Richard III as a providential design: the murder of the anointed Richard II brought a curse on England, expiated through generations of civil war and lifted only when Henry VII united the roses. Shakespeare's Richmond is deliberately idealized and lightly individualized — he enters late, prays before battle, is blessed by the ghosts, and ends the play with a vision of peace — because his dramatic function is symbolic: he embodies the restoration of order toward which the entire first tetralogy has moved. Writing under the last Tudor monarch, Shakespeare had every reason to honour the founder of her line.

cards.title: The White Boar (Richard's Badge)

source.name: Medieval English heraldry; Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
source.citation: Richard III's personal heraldic badge (cognizance) was a white boar, worn as a livery emblem by his retainers. Hence the play repeatedly calls him 'the boar' — Stanley's warning dream that 'the boar had razed his helm' (Richard III 3.2/3.4) and Richmond's 'the wretched, bloody, and usurping boar' (5.2).

cards.summary_basic: In the heraldry of the age, great lords had personal badges that their followers wore like a uniform; Richard III's badge was a white boar. That is why characters keep calling him 'the boar' rather than by name. Lord Stanley dreams that 'the boar had razed off his helm' — a warning that Richard means to behead him — and Richmond rallies his army against 'the wretched, bloody, and usurping boar.' The fierce, tusked animal is a fitting emblem for the play's predatory hero-villain.
cards.detail_scholar: A badge or 'cognizance' (distinct from the full coat of arms) identified a lord's affinity; men 'wore his livery' and badge to show whose retainers they were. The white boar was Richard's; after Bosworth, tradition holds, many boar signs on inns were hastily repainted as the blue boar of the Earl of Oxford. Shakespeare threads the badge through the play's imagery so that Richard is steadily dehumanized into a hunting-beast — 'this carnal cur,' 'that bottled spider,' 'elvish-mark'd, abortive, rooting hog,' 'the boar' — reinforcing the bestiary of curses the wronged women heap on him and preparing the final 'hunting' of Richard at Bosworth.

cards.title: The Angevin succession and Arthur's claim

source.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
source.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the sons of Henry II and the disputed succession of 1199 — John took the crown over his nephew Arthur of Brittany, son of John's elder brother Geoffrey.

cards.summary_basic: The whole quarrel of the play turns on a contested inheritance. Henry II had several sons; the crown passed to Richard I (the Lionheart), and at Richard's death in 1199 it arguably should have gone to Arthur, Duke of Brittany — son of Geoffrey, an ELDER brother of John. Instead the youngest brother, John, took the throne. France champions Arthur's senior claim, and John holds the crown (as his own mother Elinor admits) by 'strong possession' as much as by right.
cards.detail_scholar: Medieval succession was not yet fixed primogeniture: an adult brother could be preferred to a child nephew, which gave John a real, if weaker, case. John was crowned in 1199; Arthur was captured in 1202 and died — probably murdered — in 1203, and John's subsequent loss of Normandy and Anjou to France earned him the nicknames 'Lackland' and 'Softsword.' Shakespeare's play pointedly omits Magna Carta (1215) altogether, focusing on legitimacy, foreign war, and the clash with Rome rather than on the baronial liberties for which John is best remembered today. This 12th-century Angevin tangle is distinct from the later Edward III genealogy that drives the Wars of the Roses.

cards.title: King John, the Pope, and the Interdict

source.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
source.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the quarrel between King John and Pope Innocent III over Stephen Langton's election to Canterbury: the Interdict on England (1208), John's excommunication (1209), and his submission to the legate Pandulph (1213).

cards.summary_basic: John's defiance of Rome is the play's central political-religious crisis. When Pope Innocent III forced Stephen Langton on England as Archbishop of Canterbury against the king's wishes, John refused him — so the Pope laid an Interdict on the realm (closing the churches) and excommunicated the king. In the play Cardinal Pandulph, the papal legate, excommunicates John for this defiance and pressures France to make war on him; later, to save himself, John submits, surrendering his crown and receiving it back from Pandulph (3.1, 5.1).
cards.detail_scholar: Historically John defied Rome from 1207 to 1213, endured the Interdict and excommunication, and in 1213 made England a papal fief, doing homage to Innocent III through Pandulph — a humiliating about-face Shakespeare stages as cold policy. The play's John, scorning the 'Italian priest' and plundering the abbeys, was attractive to a Protestant audience as a proto-Reformation king resisting Roman tyranny (a reading the older Troublesome Raigne pushes much harder with comic friars); but Shakespeare keeps his John morally compromised — the same king who defies the Pope also murders a child. The episode is a clear forerunner of the Henry VIII break with Rome.

cards.title: Richard the Lionheart (Coeur-de-lion)

source.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
source.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Richard I 'Coeur-de-lion' (reigned 1189–1199), crusader-king and elder brother of King John, killed by a crossbow bolt at the siege of the castle of the Viscount of Limoges.

cards.summary_basic: Richard I, called Coeur-de-lion ('Lion-heart'), was John's heroic crusader brother, whose memory towers over the play. His acknowledged bastard son, Philip Faulconbridge — knighted as Sir Richard — inherits his father's lion-like courage and becomes the play's moral center. The Archduke of Austria, who wears a lion-skin, is taunted by the Bastard as the man who killed Coeur-de-lion; the Bastard kills Austria in revenge and reclaims his father's spoil.
cards.detail_scholar: Shakespeare (following the Troublesome Raigne) fuses two historical figures into the single 'Austria': Leopold V of Austria, who held Richard captive for ransom in 1192–94, and the Viscount of Limoges, by whose castle Richard took his death-wound in 1199.
