The Bastard's recovery of the lion's hide and his killing of Austria (3.2) dramatize a son avenging his father and assuming his heroic identity — the swaggering 'Cordelion' spirit reborn in the play's most vital character. The lion-skin also carries an echo of Hercules's Nemean trophy, the classic emblem of borrowed valour.

cards.title: The Troublesome Raigne of King John

source.name: The Troublesome Raigne of John, King of England (anonymous, 1591)
source.citation: Anonymous two-part play The Troublesome Raigne of John, King of England (printed 1591), Shakespeare's principal dramatic source for King John.

cards.summary_basic: Shakespeare's King John is closely based on an earlier anonymous play, The Troublesome Raigne of King John (printed 1591). The older play supplied almost the entire plot — the inheritance scene, the Bastard Faulconbridge, the siege of Angiers, Arthur's death, the clash with Rome, and John's poisoning by a monk. Shakespeare tightens the structure, deepens the characters (above all Constance and the Bastard), and tones down the cruder anti-Catholic propaganda of his source.
cards.detail_scholar: The relationship is debated — most scholars hold that Shakespeare adapted the Troublesome Raigne (c. 1589–91), though a minority argue the older play is a memorial reconstruction derived from his. The Troublesome Raigne is stridently Protestant, staging lecherous friars and a lustful nun to mock the Church; Shakespeare keeps the anti-papal politics but drops the broad satire and makes John more morally ambiguous. He also adds the verbal grandeur the source lacks — Constance's laments and the Bastard's 'commodity' (self-interest) speech — turning a propaganda chronicle-play into a study of political expediency. It belongs with Holinshed, More, and the Famous Victories among the documented source-texts behind the histories.

cards.title: The King's Great Matter (Henry's divorce)

source.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
source.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Henry VIII's suit to annul his marriage to Katherine of Aragon — the legatine court at Blackfriars (1529) under Cardinals Wolsey and Campeius, and Katherine's appeal to Rome.

cards.summary_basic: The 'King's Great Matter' was Henry VIII's long campaign to annul his twenty-year marriage to Katherine of Aragon so that he could marry Anne Bullen. Henry claimed his conscience was troubled because Katherine had first been the wife of his dead elder brother Arthur, which (he argued from Leviticus) made their union unlawful. The play dramatizes the legatine trial at Blackfriars (2.4), where Katherine defends her marriage with unanswerable dignity, refuses to accept Wolsey as her judge, and appeals to the Pope before Campeius adjourns the case to Rome.
cards.detail_scholar: Katherine of Aragon, daughter of Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain, had married Henry's brother Prince Arthur, who died months later; she then wed Henry under a papal dispensation. Henry's later 'scruple' (Leviticus 18:16, 20:21, against marrying a brother's wife) was widely seen as a pretext for his desire for Anne and a male heir. Rome's refusal to grant the annulment — Katherine's nephew was the Emperor Charles V — led directly to the break with Rome. Drawing on Holinshed, Shakespeare and Fletcher make Katherine the clear moral victor of her trial while leaving Henry's true motives studiously ambiguous.

cards.title: The break with Rome and the English Reformation

source.name: Foxe, Acts and Monuments (1583); Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
source.citation: John Foxe, Acts and Monuments (1583), and Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Henry VIII's repudiation of papal authority — the Act of Supremacy (1534) made the king Supreme Head of the Church of England, with Thomas Cranmer as Archbishop of Canterbury.

cards.summary_basic: When the Pope would not annul his marriage, Henry broke England's thousand-year obedience to Rome. By the Act of Supremacy (1534) he made himself Supreme Head of the Church of England, dissolved the monasteries, and had the reform-minded Archbishop Thomas Cranmer grant the divorce and crown Anne Bullen. The play touches this turning-point lightly but unmistakably: Cranmer's rise, and the hostility of the conservative Bishop Gardiner toward him in Act 5, reflect the religious struggle the divorce set loose.
cards.detail_scholar: Written under the Protestant-then-Stuart settlement, the play treats the Reformation with tact, since its consequences were still live. It celebrates Cranmer (later a Protestant martyr under Catholic Mary) and ends with the birth of Elizabeth, the Reformation's champion, but avoids open doctrinal polemic — unlike its source Foxe. Wolsey's fall and Cranmer's royal protection dramatize the shift of power from the old Cardinal-legate (Rome's man in England) to the new archbishop of the royal supremacy. King John's earlier defiance of the Pope was read by Tudor Protestants as a forerunner of this break.

cards.title: Cardinal Wolsey

source.name: George Cavendish, Life of Wolsey (c. 1557); Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
source.citation: George Cavendish, The Life and Death of Cardinal Wolsey (written c. 1554–57), and Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Thomas Wolsey (c. 1473–1530), Lord Chancellor and papal legate, and his fall in 1529–30.

cards.summary_basic: Thomas Wolsey, a butcher's son from Ipswich, rose to be Cardinal, Lord Chancellor, and papal legate — the most powerful man in England under Henry VIII, of almost royal magnificence (he built Hampton Court). The play traces his pride and fall: he destroys Buckingham, drives the divorce, and amasses huge wealth, until intercepted letters and an inventory of his riches expose his double-dealing. Stripped of office, he takes his celebrated farewell to 'all my greatness' and dies humbled (3.2).
cards.detail_scholar: Wolsey's failure to win the annulment from Rome ruined him: charged under praemunire (for asserting papal authority within the realm), he surrendered his goods, was arrested for treason, and died at Leicester Abbey in 1530 on his way to London. Shakespeare's sympathetic portrait of the fallen Cardinal — including the famous dying sentiment that had he served God as zealously as the king, God would not have left him 'naked to mine enemies' — draws on the intimate Life by his gentleman-usher George Cavendish. Griffith's even-handed obituary (4.2) credits Wolsey's vices and his virtues alike (he founded colleges at Oxford and Ipswich). His rise-and-fall is the play's central instance of the de casibus pattern.

cards.title: Foxe's Acts and Monuments (Book of Martyrs)

source.name: John Foxe, Acts and Monuments (1563; expanded 1583)
source.citation: John Foxe, Acts and Monuments of these Latter and Perilous Days (first English edition 1563; expanded 1583) — the great Protestant martyrology, a source for the Cranmer material in Henry VIII Act 5.

cards.summary_basic: Foxe's Acts and Monuments — popularly the 'Book of Martyrs' — was, after the Bible, the most influential book in Protestant England: a vast history of the Church told as the struggle of true believers against papal persecution. It supplied Henry VIII with its Act 5 material on Archbishop Cranmer — the plot of the conservative bishops to destroy him and his rescue by the king (the ring, the council scene) come from Foxe. Copies were chained in churches, and its martyr-stories shaped how the audience understood the Reformation.
cards.detail_scholar: Foxe celebrated Cranmer, burned under Catholic Mary in 1556, as a Protestant hero, and his account of the Henrician court furnished the dramatists with the 5.1–5.3 episode almost intact. The play's providential Protestant frame — climaxing in Cranmer's prophecy over the infant Elizabeth — is broadly Foxean, though Shakespeare and Fletcher mute the militant anti-Catholicism of their source. Foxe's authority helps explain why an English audience would readily accept Cranmer as the saintly counterweight to Bishop Gardiner.

cards.title: The Field of the Cloth of Gold

source.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
source.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the summit between Henry VIII and Francis I of France near Calais (the 'Field of the Cloth of Gold'), June 1520.

cards.summary_basic: The play opens with Norfolk's dazzled account of the Field of the Cloth of Gold — the spectacularly lavish summit of 1520 where Henry VIII and the young French king Francis I met near Calais in a fortnight-long contest of magnificence, with cloth-of-gold tents, tournaments, and feasting (1.1). Buckingham observes that Cardinal Wolsey stage-managed the whole ruinous extravagance, and that the peace it celebrated was already crumbling — introducing both Wolsey's overweening power and the play's theme of dazzling pomp over substance.
cards.detail_scholar: The 1520 meeting near Guisnes and Ardres (the play's 'Guynes and Arde') cost both crowns enormous sums and sealed an Anglo-French amity that collapsed within two years when Henry allied instead with the Emperor Charles V. Shakespeare uses Norfolk's set-piece description to establish a world of costly ceremony and to plant the nobles' resentment of the low-born Cardinal who 'order'd' such grandeur, as Buckingham complains, largely 'without the privity o' the king.' The episode sets the play's recurring contrast between glittering show and the hard realities of power.

cards.title: Cranmer's prophecy over the infant Elizabeth

source.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587); the play's own invention
source.citation: Henry VIII 5.5; the christening of Princess Elizabeth (later Elizabeth I), 10 September 1533. The prophecy is the dramatists' invention, written in hindsight from the reigns of Elizabeth (d. 1603) and James I.

cards.summary_basic: The play climaxes with the christening of the infant Elizabeth, over whom Archbishop Cranmer delivers a prophecy (5.5): the child will be a 'pattern to all princes,' bringing an age of peace and plenty, and like a phoenix her greatness will pass undimmed to a successor. For Shakespeare's audience this was history foretold — Elizabeth I had been their long-reigned queen, and the promised 'heir' is a flattering nod to the reigning James I. The scene turns a court chronicle into a celebration of the Tudor–Stuart providential destiny.
cards.detail_scholar: The prophecy is panegyric written with hindsight — the play dates to 1613, a decade into James's reign. Cranmer promises that Elizabeth shall be 'a pattern to all princes,' a 'maiden phoenix' from whose ashes a new heir (James) shall rise 'as great in admiration as herself.' It weaves in biblical images of peace — every man safe 'under his own vine what he plants' (echoing Micah 4:4 and 1 Kings 4:25) — and the wisdom of the Queen of Sheba ('Saba'). Retroactively it frames the whole turbulent reign of Henry VIII as the providential prelude to England's golden age, aligning the play with the larger Tudor myth.

cards.title: The Bermuda wreck of the Sea Venture (1609)

source.name: Strachey, A True Reportory (1610); Jourdain, Discovery of the Barmudas (1610)
source.citation: William Strachey, 'A True Reportory of the Wracke and Redemption of Sir Thomas Gates, Knight' (letter dated 15 July 1610; printed 1625 in Purchas His Pilgrimes); Sylvester Jourdain, 'A Discovery of the Barmudas' (1610). The Sea Venture wrecked on Bermuda in a hurricane, July 1609. Cf. The Tempest 1.2, 'the still-vex'd Bermoothes.'

cards.summary_basic: In 1609 the Sea Venture, flagship of a fleet bound for the Virginia colony, was driven by a hurricane onto the reefs of Bermuda; all aboard survived, wintered on the supposedly devil-haunted island, built two new ships, and reached Jamestown in 1610. Eyewitness accounts — chiefly William Strachey's letter — reached London just as Shakespeare wrote The Tempest, and are its most-cited topical source: the tempest, the 'still-vex'd Bermoothes,' the fire on the rigging, and the miraculously unharmed castaways all echo the reports.
cards.detail_scholar: Strachey's 'True Reportory' (written 1610, not printed until 1625, so Shakespeare likely read it in manuscript) describes a storm of exactly the play's kind, the eerie fire Ariel evokes when he 'flam'd amazement' on the rigging (St Elmo's fire), the abundance of the uninhabited island, and quarrels and a mutiny among the stranded men — analogues to the Stephano-Caliban plot. Bermuda was reputed an 'Ile of Divels.' Shakespeare moves his island to the Mediterranean, but Ariel's errand to fetch dew 'from the still-vex'd Bermoothes' (1.2) winks at the source. The episode also ties the play to the Virginia Company's colonial enterprise, the backdrop to its nature-and-empire themes.

cards.title: Montaigne, 'Of the Cannibals'

source.name: Montaigne, Essais (Florio's translation, 1603)
source.citation: Michel de Montaigne, 'Of the Cannibals' (Des Cannibales, Essais I.31), in John Florio's English translation, 1603. Gonzalo's ideal-commonwealth speech, The Tempest 2.1.148-169, paraphrases it directly.

cards.summary_basic: Montaigne's essay 'Of the Cannibals' (c. 1580; Englished by John Florio in 1603) argues that the 'savage' peoples of the New World live closer to virtuous nature than civilized Europeans, who are the real barbarians. Shakespeare knew Florio's version: Gonzalo's daydream of an ideal commonwealth with 'no kind of traffic... no name of magistrate... no occupation' (2.1) lifts a whole passage almost word for word, and the essay feeds the play's debate over nature, culture, and who is truly 'civil.'
cards.detail_scholar: Florio's Montaigne describes a nation that has 'no kinde of traffike, no knowledge of letters, no intelligence of numbers, no name of magistrate, nor of politike superioritie' — Gonzalo's speech follows it clause by clause, then is mocked by Antonio and Sebastian ('The latter end of his commonwealth forgets the beginning'). The essay's larger claim — that European 'civility' may be more barbarous than the cannibals' simplicity — runs through the Prospero-Caliban relationship and the play's questioning of nature versus nurture. The name 'Caliban' is widely read as an anagram or near-echo of 'cannibal' (itself from 'Carib'). Montaigne is one of the play's two firmest topical sources, alongside the Bermuda narratives.

cards.title: Setebos, Caliban's god

source.name: Pigafetta's Magellan voyage, in Eden's History of Travel (1577)
source.citation: Antonio Pigafetta's account of Magellan's 1520 voyage, Englished in Richard Eden, 'The History of Travayle in the West and East Indies' (1577): the Patagonian 'giants' invoke a great devil, 'Setebos.' Caliban swears by 'Setebos, my dam's god' (The Tempest 1.2; cf. 5.1).

cards.summary_basic: Setebos was a god — reported as a 'great devil' — of the Patagonians of South America, recorded by a survivor of Magellan's circumnavigation and printed in English in Richard Eden's 1577 collection of travel narratives. Shakespeare borrowed the exotic name for the deity of Caliban's witch-mother Sycorax: Caliban fears Prospero's art 'would control my dam's god, Setebos' (1.2), and at the end marvels, 'O Setebos, these be brave spirits indeed!' (5.1).
cards.detail_scholar: The name comes from one of the era's most widely read travel books: Eden's translation of Pigafetta's report that the towering 'giants' of Patagonia, when seized, roared upon their god Setebos. Its appearance in The Tempest is a small but telling sign of how the play absorbs New World voyage literature: Caliban's religion is given a real, documented 'savage' deity, locating Sycorax's witchcraft in the same ethnographic imagination as the Bermuda and Montaigne material. It is among the clearest verbal borrowings from the travel narratives in the play.

cards.title: John Gower and the Confessio Amantis

source.name: John Gower, Confessio Amantis (c. 1390)
source.citation: John Gower, Confessio Amantis (c. 1390), Book 8 — the tale of Apollonius of Tyre, the main source of Pericles. The poet appears 'as Chorus' and narrates the play.

cards.summary_basic: John Gower (c. 1330-1408) was a major English poet, a friend of Chaucer, whose long poem Confessio Amantis ('The Lover's Confession') retells the ancient romance of Apollonius of Tyre — the story Pericles dramatizes. Shakespeare brings the poet himself onstage as the Presenter, 'ancient Gower... from ashes,' who speaks an old-fashioned rhymed chorus before every act, introduces the silent dumb-shows, and points the moral at the close.
cards.detail_scholar: Using Gower as Chorus is a deliberate antiquarian effect: his pointedly archaic four-beat couplets ('To sing a song that old was sung, / From ashes ancient Gower is come') signal that the audience is hearing a venerable medieval tale, one 'sung at festivals, / On ember-eves and holy-ales.' Gower bridges the play's huge leaps of time and place ('I do beseech you / To learn of me, who stand i' the gaps to teach you'), turning the episodic, decades-spanning romance into a narrated story-within-a-frame and using dumb-shows to compress action he then glosses 'with speech.' The device shaped both the play's old reputation as a 'mouldy tale' and its modern revival as a sophisticated experiment in storytelling.

cards.title: The romance of Apollonius of Tyre

source.name: Historia Apollonii regis Tyri; Twine, The Patterne of Painefull Adventures (1576)
source.citation: The anonymous Latin romance 'Historia Apollonii regis Tyri' (c. 5th-6th century AD); Englished by Laurence Twine as 'The Patterne of Painefull Adventures' (c. 1576, reprinted 1607), Shakespeare's source alongside Gower's Confessio Amantis.

cards.summary_basic: Behind Pericles lies one of the most popular stories of the Middle Ages: the Latin romance of Apollonius of Tyre — a prince driven by shipwreck and fortune across the Mediterranean, parted from his wife and daughter and reunited with them years later. Shakespeare follows it through two English versions, Gower's poem and Laurence Twine's prose 'Patterne of Painefull Adventures,' changing the hero's name from Apollonius to Pericles.
cards.detail_scholar: The 'Historia Apollonii regis Tyri' survives in dozens of medieval manuscripts and languages; its episodic shape — a riddle of incest, storms, apparent deaths, a daughter preserved in a brothel by her virtue, and a recognition scene and temple reunion — is the skeleton of Pericles. Twine's prose redaction (entered 1576, reprinted 1607, just as the play was written) supplied much narrative detail, while Gower's verse supplied the frame. Shakespeare's renaming of Apollonius as 'Pericles' may glance at the noble Pyrocles of Sidney's Arcadia. The play's collaborative text (likely Shakespeare with George Wilkins, who also issued a 1608 prose 'Painfull Adventures of Pericles') reflects this layered descent.

cards.title: Ancient Britain and the Roman tribute

source.name: Holinshed, Chronicles; Julius Caesar, Gallic War; Suetonius
source.citation: Holinshed's Chronicles (1587), History of England, on Kymbeline (Cunobeline) and Britain's tribute to Rome; Julius Caesar, Gallic War 4-5 (the British expeditions of 55-54 BC and the tribute imposed on Cassibelan); the reign of Augustus. Cymbeline's refusal of the tribute 'left by Julius Caesar' (3.1, 3.5) provokes the play's war with Rome, healed by the renewed peace of 5.5.

cards.summary_basic: The play's British frame is loosely historical. The real Cunobeline ('Cymbeline') ruled south-east Britain in the early first century AD. Julius Caesar had invaded Britain in 55-54 BC and imposed a yearly tribute; in the play Cymbeline's queen and son goad him into refusing it ('Britain is a world by itself'), provoking a Roman invasion in the age of Augustus. Shakespeare took the outline from Holinshed but set it, deliberately, at the moment of universal peace into which Christ was born.
cards.detail_scholar: Holinshed gave Shakespeare Kymbeline, said to have been raised at Augustus's court, and the dispute over a tribute first owed to Caesar; the dramatist then reshaped it freely. The defiant speeches about Britain 'ribb'd and pal'd in / With rocks unscalable and roaring waters' (3.1) voice a Jacobean island patriotism, while the ending — Cymbeline freely paying the tribute he has just defeated Rome to avoid — images a reconciliation of British independence with the Pax Romana (and flatters James I's claim to a peace-bringing, Britain-uniting kingship). The same legendary-British, Holinshed-derived material underlies King Lear.

cards.title: Milford Haven

source.name: Holinshed, Chronicles; Tudor dynastic history
source.citation: Milford Haven, the great natural harbour in Pembrokeshire, west Wales. In Cymbeline it is the goal toward which nearly every character converges (3.2-5.1). Historically the landing-place of Henry Tudor, earl of Richmond (the future Henry VII), in August 1485 before his victory at Bosworth — the origin of the Tudor dynasty whose line James I claimed to continue.

cards.summary_basic: Milford Haven is a large, sheltered harbour in west Wales. In Cymbeline it becomes a magnetic destination: Pisanio's letter lures Imogen there to meet Posthumus, Cloten pursues her toward it, and the Roman army lands there. To a Jacobean audience the name carried a charge — it was where Henry Tudor landed in 1485 to win the crown at Bosworth and found the dynasty — so Wales and Milford evoke British destiny and the Welsh roots of the Tudor-Stuart line.
cards.detail_scholar: Shakespeare's insistence on the name — Imogen's rapturous question 'how far it is / To this same blessed Milford' (3.2) — has long struck readers as more than geography. Writing for James I, who styled himself a second Brutus uniting the whole island, Shakespeare lets the harbour where the Welsh Henry Tudor began the dynasty become the place where Cymbeline's scattered family, and Britain's quarrel with Rome, are mended. The wild Welsh mountains around it also serve the old romance motif of the remote place where lost royal children are hidden and at last found.

cards.title: Giulio Romano, the statue's maker

source.name: Giorgio Vasari, Lives of the Most Excellent Painters (1550, 1568)
source.citation: Giulio Romano (c. 1499-1546), Italian painter and architect, the foremost pupil of Raphael. In The Winter's Tale 5.2 Hermione's lifelike 'statue' is said to be 'a piece many years in doing and now newly performed by that rare Italian master, Julio Romano.' Vasari's Lives celebrated him and quoted a Latin epitaph claiming his figures seemed to breathe.

cards.summary_basic: Giulio Romano was a real Renaissance Italian artist, a leading pupil of Raphael. In Act 5 the gentlemen report that Hermione's astonishingly lifelike statue was made by 'that rare Italian master, Julio Romano' — a striking anachronism, since the story is set in a pagan antiquity centuries before he lived. Naming a famous modern sculptor sharpens the wonder of the scene in which the 'statue' proves to be the living queen.
cards.detail_scholar: This is Shakespeare's only explicit naming of a Renaissance visual artist. Giorgio Vasari's Lives of the Artists praised Giulio Romano, and an epitaph Vasari quoted boasted that his sculpted and painted figures seemed almost to live and breathe — exactly the illusion the play stages when Paulina unveils a statue so lifelike that Leontes thinks it breathes and stirs, then bids it 'be stone no more.' The anachronism belongs to the romance's deliberate blend of pagan oracle and Renaissance art, and glances at the period's lively debate (the paragone) over whether painting or sculpture could best rival life itself.

cards.title: Falconry and the taming of the haggard

source.name: George Turbervile, The Booke of Faulconrie or Hawking (1575)
source.citation: George Turbervile, The Booke of Faulconrie or Hawking (London, 1575); Edmund Bert, An Approved Treatise of Hawkes and Hawking (London, 1619). In The Taming of the Shrew 4.1 Petruchio's soliloquy makes his taming of Katherina a sustained falconry conceit: 'My falcon now is sharp and passing empty, / And till she stoop she must not be full-gorg'd... / Another way I have to man my haggard.'

cards.summary_basic: Falconry — hunting with trained hawks — was a prestige sport with its own technical vocabulary. 'Manning' a wild-caught hawk (a 'haggard') meant taming it by keeping it hungry and sleepless ('watching') until it would answer the falconer's call and 'stoop' (swoop) to the baited 'lure.' Petruchio frames his whole campaign against Katherina in exactly these terms.
cards.detail_scholar: In 4.1 the conceit is explicit and unbroken: a 'haggard' is an adult wild-caught female hawk (proverbially hard to tame); to 'man' it is to accustom it to the human hand; to be 'full-gorg'd' is to be fed to satiety, after which a hawk ignores the lure — so Petruchio keeps Kate hungry, 'sharp and passing empty,' and sleepless ('she ate no meat to-day, nor none shall eat; / Last night she slept not, nor to-night she shall not'), the standard manning regime, ending 'This is a way to kill a wife with kindness.' The image casts the wife as a wild bird brought to her 'keeper's call.' Shakespeare uses haggard-imagery for women elsewhere — Othello's 'If I do prove her haggard' (3.3), Hero a 'haggard of the rock' in Much Ado (3.1) — so the falconry frame would have read at once to an audience for whom hawking was familiar.

cards.title: Patient Griselda

source.name: Boccaccio, Decameron; Chaucer, The Clerk's Tale
source.citation: Boccaccio, Decameron 10.10 (1353); Petrarch's Latin retelling (1373); Chaucer, The Canterbury Tales, The Clerk's Tale (c. 1390). In The Taming of the Shrew 2.1 Petruchio predicts that Katherina 'for patience... will prove a second Grissel, / And Roman Lucrece for her chastity.'

cards.summary_basic: Griselda (Grissel) was the medieval type of the perfectly patient, obedient wife: a poor woman married by a marquis who tests her submission with appalling cruelty — pretending to kill her children, pretending to cast her off — all of which she bears without a word of complaint. Her name was Elizabethan shorthand for wifely meekness, the very opposite of the 'curst' Katherina.
cards.detail_scholar: Petruchio's claim that Kate will prove 'a second Grissel' (2.1) is heavy irony at the moment he first meets her fury. The story reached England through Boccaccio's Decameron, Petrarch's influential Latin version, and above all Chaucer's Clerk's Tale, and it sets the ideal of the silently obedient wife against which the play's 'taming' — and Katherina's contested closing speech on a wife's duty (5.2) — must be measured. Where Griselda's obedience is saintly and unbroken, Kate's is won by hunger and contradiction, and modern readers debate whether her final submission is sincere, strategic, or staged.

cards.title: The sleeper awakened (the beggar made a lord)

source.name: Simon Goulart, Admirable and Memorable Histories (trans. Grimeston, 1607)
source.citation: The motif of the poor man made drunk and persuaded he is a lord: told of Duke Philip the Good of Burgundy in Simon Goulart, Admirable and Memorable Histories (trans. E. Grimeston, 1607), and in the Arabian Nights tale 'The Sleeper Awakened' (folk-tale type Aarne-Thompson-Uther 1531). The Induction of The Taming of the Shrew (Induction 1-2) stages this trick on the tinker Christopher Sly.

cards.summary_basic: The Induction's joke — a drunken beggar dressed as a lord and convinced his real life was only a dream — is an old, much-travelled story. Versions appear in the Arabian Nights ('The Sleeper Awakened') and in a popular anecdote about Duke Philip the Good of Burgundy, who is said to have played exactly this trick on a sleeping artisan.
cards.detail_scholar: Shakespeare frames the entire comedy as a play staged for the gulled tinker Christopher Sly. In the Folio text Sly never reappears to be undeceived — the frame is left open — whereas the related anonymous play The Taming of A Shrew (1594) closes it, sending Sly home cured of his 'dream' and resolved to tame his own wife. The motif of the beggar woken into false lordship, and the teasing question of which life is the dream, rhymes with the disguises, role-playing, and 'supposes' (mistaken identities) of the Padua comedy that follows.

cards.title: The Nine Worthies

source.name: Jacques de Longuyon, Les Voeux du Paon (c. 1312); William Caxton
source.citation: The Nine Worthies, a standard medieval and Renaissance set of nine model heroes — three pagan (Hector, Alexander the Great, Julius Caesar), three Jewish (Joshua, David, Judas Maccabaeus), three Christian (King Arthur, Charlemagne, Godfrey of Bouillon) — first catalogued in Jacques de Longuyon's Les Voeux du Paon (c. 1312). In Love's Labour's Lost 5.1-5.2 Holofernes stages a botched pageant of the Worthies.

cards.summary_basic: The 'Nine Worthies' were a familiar set of nine ideal heroes of chivalry — three from pagan antiquity, three from the Hebrew Bible, and three from Christian history — paraded in medieval and Tudor pageants as the very models of honour. In Love's Labour's Lost a troupe of village amateurs stages a pageant of the Worthies that falls comically apart as the players forget and muddle their parts.
cards.detail_scholar: The canonical nine were Hector, Alexander, and Julius Caesar; Joshua, David, and Judas Maccabaeus; and Arthur, Charlemagne, and Godfrey of Bouillon. Holofernes's amateur cast bungles even the line-up — putting forward Pompey (Costard) and the infant Hercules (the boy Moth) in place of proper Worthies, while Armado plays Hector, the curate Nathaniel plays Alexander, and Holofernes himself plays Judas Maccabaeus, only to be heckled with jokes confusing him with Judas Iscariot. The disintegrating pageant mirrors the play's larger pattern: grand performances of learning and honour undone by human folly. The Worthies were common stage and pageant fare, and Shakespeare glances at them elsewhere (2 Henry IV 2.4).

cards.title: The masque of Muscovites

source.name: Edward Hall, Chronicle (1548); Gesta Grayorum (1594-95)
source.citation: Court 'disguisings' of exotic strangers were a Tudor commonplace: Hall's Chronicle records Henry VIII and his courtiers masking 'apparelled after the manner of Russia or Muscovy' at Christmas 1510, and the Gray's Inn Christmas revels of 1594-95 (recorded in Gesta Grayorum) staged a mock embassy from Russia. In Love's Labour's Lost 5.2 the King and lords woo the ladies disguised as Russians ('Muscovites').

cards.summary_basic: In Act 5 the King and his lords approach the ladies disguised as 'Muscovites' — Russians — a fashionable kind of court masque in which gentlemen entered in exotic costume to dance and woo. Forewarned by Boyet, the masked ladies swap the love-tokens the men sent, so each lord courts the wrong woman and is mercilessly mocked; the grand performance collapses.
cards.detail_scholar: Disguising as foreign 'strangers' — Turks, blackamoors, Russians — was a stock device of the Tudor court masque (Hall records Henry VIII masking as a Muscovite in 1510). The choice of Russians was topical: the Muscovy Company (chartered 1555) and the exchange of embassies between Elizabeth I and Ivan the Terrible had made far-off Muscovy a byword for the strange and remote, and the Gray's Inn revels of 1594-95 — close to the play's date — featured just such a mock-Russian show. The scene satirises the empty theatricality of the lords' wooing: their elaborate 'masque' is seen through at once, and the ladies turn the men's own performance against them.

cards.title: The Fable of the Belly and the Members

source.name: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita; Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus (North 1579)
source.citation: Aesop, Fables (the Belly and the Members); Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 2.32; Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus 6.

cards.summary_basic: Menenius quiets the rioting plebeians in 1.1 with an old fable: the body's other parts once rebelled against the belly, thinking it idle and greedy, and refused to feed it — and so starved themselves, since the belly digests and sends nourishment to every limb. The belly stands for the Senate and patricians; the mutinous members are the people. The parable defends Rome's hierarchy as a single, mutually dependent body.
cards.detail_scholar: The fable is Aesopic, but Shakespeare follows Livy (2.32) and Plutarch's Life of Coriolanus, where Menenius Agrippa uses it to end the first secession of the plebs (494 BCE). The 'body politic' — the state as one body whose head, belly, and limbs all need one another — was a Renaissance commonplace of political theory. Menenius casts the patricians as the nourishing belly and the citizens as ungrateful limbs; the First Citizen cuts back by naming Marcius 'the great toe of this assembly.' Written amid the Midlands grain riots of 1607, the scene gives the ancient class quarrel a contemporary edge.

cards.title: The Tribunes of the People

source.name: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita; Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus
source.citation: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 2.32-33; Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus 7 (the tribunate created after the plebeian secession, 494 BCE).

cards.summary_basic: After the common people (plebeians) walked out of Rome in protest, the patricians agreed to a new office: the tribunes of the people, elected magistrates whose persons were declared sacrosanct and who could block official acts to protect plebeian interests. Sicinius and Brutus are two such tribunes; the play turns on the new, resented power they wield against the patrician Coriolanus.
cards.detail_scholar: The tribunate (traditionally 494 BCE, per Livy) was won in the 'Conflict of the Orders,' the long struggle between patricians and plebeians. A tribune was legally untouchable and could veto (intercessio) consuls, senate, and other magistrates. Coriolanus regards giving the people such a voice as the ruin of the state: 'my soul aches / To know, when two authorities are up, / Neither supreme, how soon confusion / May enter' (3.1). Shakespeare, writing during the 1607 Midlands enclosure riots, gives the Roman class conflict a sharp contemporary charge.

cards.title: The Consulship and the Gown of Humility

source.name: Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus (North 1579); Livy, Ab Urbe Condita
source.citation: Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus 14-15; Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 2.33-35 (the canvass for the consulship).

cards.summary_basic: The consulship was the Republic's highest office — two consuls, elected each year, holding supreme civil and military power. A candidate (Latin candidatus, from the white toga he wore) had to canvass the people in the Forum, traditionally in a plain 'gown of humility,' and to show the scars he had won for Rome, to earn their 'voices' (votes). Named consul by the Senate, Coriolanus can scarcely endure this ritual of begging the commoners he despises.
cards.detail_scholar: Plutarch describes the custom: candidates went to the Forum in a loose toga without a tunic, 'either because they would seem humble ... or that they might show their wounds.' Coriolanus's revulsion at displaying his scars and soliciting the plebeians' suffrages — 'Why in this woolvish toge should I stand here, / To beg of Hob and Dick?' (2.3) — and the tribunes' manipulation of the granted-then-revoked vote drive the play's central crisis. Throughout the play 'voices' means votes; the consul-elect must be confirmed by the people he has just been forced to court.

cards.title: The Volscians, Corioli, and Antium

source.name: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita; Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus
source.citation: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 2.33-40; Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus 8-11, 22-24 (the Volscian wars and the surname 'Coriolanus').

cards.summary_basic: The Volscians were an Italic people of central Italy, Rome's persistent enemies in the early Republic. Caius Marcius wins his surname 'Coriolanus' by storming their city of Corioli; later, banished from Rome, he takes refuge in their chief city Antium with their general Aufidius and leads their army against Rome itself.
cards.detail_scholar: Rome and the Volscians fought repeatedly through the fifth century BCE. Plutarch and Livy record that Marcius was given the honorific surname Coriolanus for his valour at the capture of Corioli (traditionally 493 BCE). Antium (modern Anzio) was the Volscians' principal town and Aufidius's home, where the disguised Coriolanus offers himself at 'Aufidius' hearth' (4.5). Shakespeare follows Plutarch's geography closely while sharpening the personal rivalry of Coriolanus and Aufidius into the play's central duel — the soldier who cannot live within Rome's politics, destroyed first by Rome and then by Rome's enemy.

cards.title: Virginius and the death of Virginia

source.name: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita
source.citation: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 3.44-58 (the centurion Virginius kills his daughter Virginia, c. 449 BCE, rather than let the decemvir Appius Claudius seize her). Titus invokes the precedent before killing Lavinia (5.3).

cards.summary_basic: In a famous Roman story, the centurion Virginius stabbed his own daughter Virginia to death rather than let the corrupt magistrate Appius Claudius seize and dishonour her; the outrage helped topple the tyrannical decemvirs and restore the Republic. At the final banquet Titus asks whether Virginius did right 'to slay his daughter with his own right hand, / Because she was enforced, stain'd, and deflower'd,' and then kills the ravished Lavinia on that precedent.
cards.detail_scholar: Livy (3.44-58) tells how Appius Claudius schemed to enslave the free-born Virginia; her father killed her in the Forum to keep her free and unstained, and the revolt that followed brought down the decemvirate. Titus treats the killing as a model of fatherly honour, formally asking the emperor's assent to the 'reason' (5.3) before he kills Lavinia to end both her shame and his grief. The episode shows the play's Roman ethic at its most chilling — a daughter's life weighed against the family's honour — and pairs with the Lucrece story, the other Roman exemplum of a violated woman's death.

cards.title: Seneca and the revenge tragedy

source.name: Seneca, Thyestes; Seneca His Tenne Tragedies (1581)
source.citation: Seneca, Thyestes (Atreus tricks Thyestes into eating his own sons at a banquet); the English Senecan vogue via Jasper Heywood's translations and Thomas Newton's collection Seneca His Tenne Tragedies (1581).

cards.summary_basic: The Roman playwright Seneca wrote blood-soaked tragedies of revenge, ghosts, tyranny, and high rhetoric — among them Thyestes, in which a man is tricked into eating his own children at a feast. Englished in 1581 and hugely influential, Seneca set the template for Elizabethan revenge tragedy. Titus Andronicus is Shakespeare's most Senecan play: its on-stage horrors, its ranting grief, and above all Titus's banquet of Tamora's baked sons descend directly from Thyestes.
cards.detail_scholar: Senecan drama gave the English stage its revenge plot, its taste for spectacular on-stage atrocity and sententious declamation, and stock devices such as the ghost crying for vengeance. The Thyestean banquet — Atreus feeding Thyestes his sons — is the explicit model for Titus's revenge on Tamora, just as Ovid's Procne (who serves Tereus their son) is the mythic one. Kyd's roughly contemporary The Spanish Tragedy shares the mode; together these plays launched the revenge-tragedy boom that runs through to Hamlet.

cards.title: The 'Moor' on the Elizabethan stage

source.name: Elizabethan stage convention; Leo Africanus, A Geographical Historie of Africa (trans. Pory, 1600)
source.citation: The stage figure of the 'Moor': cf. Aaron (Titus Andronicus), the Prince of Morocco (Merchant of Venice), and Othello. Context: Queen Elizabeth's proclamations against 'blackamoors' (1596, 1601) and travel writing such as Leo Africanus, Englished by John Pory in 1600.

cards.summary_basic: 'Moor' was a loose Elizabethan word for North Africans, sub-Saharan Africans, and Muslims generally, and the stage often tied dark skin to villainy and the demonic. Aaron is the theatre's early example of the type, and the play heaps racist contempt on him — 'barbarous Moor,' 'irreligious' — language it puts in the mouths of its Roman characters. Yet Shakespeare also gives Aaron wit, self-knowledge, and a fierce love for his infant son, complicating the stereotype even while using it.
cards.detail_scholar: The English stage Moor descended partly from the black-faced devils of the medieval mystery plays and from the Vice of the morality drama; Aaron's gleeful, audience-confiding villainy is close kin to the Vice. Shakespeare returns to the figure in the Prince of Morocco and, transformingly, in Othello, where the Moor is the tragic hero rather than the villain. The play's racism is best treated as a historical attitude it dramatizes — Aaron is despised for his colour by Romans who are themselves monstrous — not as the play's endorsed view; his defence of his black child ('Is black so base a hue?', 4.2) turns the prejudice back on Rome.

cards.title: The Battle of Actium

source.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony
source.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 63-68 (the sea-battle off Actium, 2 September 31 BCE).

cards.summary_basic: Actium was the decisive sea-battle of the Roman civil war, fought off the western coast of Greece on 2 September 31 BCE. Antony, persuaded against his soldiers' advice to fight at sea, was beaten by Octavius's admiral Agrippa; when Cleopatra's squadron of sixty ships suddenly turned and fled, Antony broke off the battle to follow her, throwing away his cause. The play dramatizes the disaster across the short scenes of Act 3 (3.7-3.10).
cards.detail_scholar: Plutarch reports the same fatal sequence: Cleopatra's ships hoisting sail and fleeing, and Antony following 'as if he had been glued unto her,' a man 'carried away with the vain love of this woman as if he had been... not master of himself.' Shakespeare's Scarus captures the shame — 'The greater cantle of the world is lost... / We have kiss'd away / Kingdoms and provinces.' Actium left Octavius master of the Roman world and led, within a year, to the fall of Alexandria and the deaths of both lovers.

cards.title: The asp (Cleopatra's death)

source.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony; Pliny, Natural History
source.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 85-86 (the asp brought in a basket of figs, 30 BCE); cf. Pliny, Natural History 8.35 on the Egyptian asp.

cards.summary_basic: The asp was a venomous Egyptian snake (probably the cobra). Plutarch reports that Cleopatra, resolved not to be led through Rome in Octavius's triumph, had an asp smuggled to her in a basket of figs and died of its bite — a death held to be painless, even sleep-like. Shakespeare follows him: a Clown brings 'the pretty worm of Nilus' hidden among figs (5.2), and Cleopatra applies it to her breast and arm.
cards.detail_scholar: Plutarch admits the exact means was uncertain — an asp, or a poisoned pin hidden in her hair — but the asp became the canonical image. The snake carried Egyptian royal symbolism: the rearing uraeus-cobra adorned the pharaoh's crown, so the manner of death reads as a final assertion of sovereignty against Rome. Cleopatra's 'Dost thou not see my baby at my breast / That sucks the nurse asleep?' fuses death, motherhood, and the nurturing goddess Isis into a single image.

cards.title: The Ptolemies and Egypt

source.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony; Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca historica
source.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony; Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca historica 1 (on Egypt). The Ptolemaic dynasty ruled Egypt 305-30 BCE.

cards.summary_basic: Cleopatra was the last ruler of the Ptolemies, a Macedonian-Greek dynasty founded by one of Alexander the Great's generals that had governed Egypt since 305 BCE. To Romans, Egypt was fabulously rich, ancient, and 'oriental' — a land of the flooding Nile, of luxury, and of god-kings — everything the austere Roman republic claimed not to be. The play builds its whole structure on this Egypt-versus-Rome opposition.
cards.detail_scholar: The Ptolemies ruled as pharaohs, taking up Egyptian divine kingship (and dynastic sibling-marriage); Cleopatra VII, unusually, learned the Egyptian language and styled herself the New Isis. Rome both coveted Egypt's wealth — its grain helped feed the city — and feared its monarchy as the antithesis of republican virtue. Antony's 'donations of Alexandria,' parcelling out eastern kingdoms to Cleopatra and their children (3.6), handed Octavius the propaganda he needed to recast the civil war as Rome's war against a foreign queen.

cards.title: The Second Triumvirate

source.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony; Suetonius, Divus Augustus
source.citation: Plutarch, Lives (Antony, Caesar); Suetonius, Divus Augustus. The triumvirate of Antony, Octavian, and Lepidus, established 43 BCE.

cards.summary_basic: After Julius Caesar's murder, his heir Octavius joined Antony and Lepidus in 43 BCE in a legally constituted three-man commission to rule the state and avenge Caesar — the Second Triumvirate. They divided the Roman world among themselves and proscribed (outlawed and killed) their enemies. The play opens with this uneasy partnership already fraying: Antony is 'the triple pillar of the world,' one of 'these three world-sharers.'
cards.detail_scholar: The triumvirate was always a holding pattern before a final reckoning. Lepidus, the weakest, was stripped of his power by Octavius in 36 BCE (reported at 3.5); Sextus Pompey, who controlled the seas, was bought off at Misenum (2.6) and later destroyed; that left Antony and Octavius to fight for sole mastery at Actium. Shakespeare compresses a decade of manoeuvre into the play's first three acts, keeping the focus on the personal rivalry beneath the politics.

cards.title: Octavius, Augustus, and the universal peace

source.name: Suetonius, Divus Augustus; Virgil, Aeneid
source.citation: Suetonius, Divus Augustus 22 (the closing of the gates of Janus); Virgil, Aeneid 1.286-296. Octavius took the name 'Augustus' in 27 BCE.

cards.summary_basic: By defeating Antony, Octavius became sole ruler of Rome and, in 27 BCE, took the name Augustus — in effect the first Roman emperor. His long reign brought the 'Pax Romana,' a celebrated era of peace after a century of civil war. In the play Octavius foresees it on the eve of victory: 'The time of universal peace is near' (4.6), when 'the three-nook'd world / Shall bear the olive freely.'
cards.detail_scholar: Augustus advertised the new peace by ceremonially closing the temple of Janus, shut only when Rome was wholly at peace. For Shakespeare's audience the Augustan peace also carried a providential charge: it was the reign in which 'there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus' (Luke 2:1) and Christ was born — so the cold, calculating victor of this tragedy was also, in the Renaissance historical imagination, the emperor under whom the world fell briefly and totally quiet. The line lends Octavius's triumph a chilly, world-historical weight.

cards.title: The weird sisters and Jacobean witchcraft

source.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (Scotland); James VI and I, Daemonologie
source.citation: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), History of Scotland (the 'weird sisters' who meet Macbeth and Banquo); James VI and I, Daemonologie (1597); the Witchcraft Act of 1604.

cards.summary_basic: The three witches are the 'weird sisters' — 'weird' is from the Old English 'wyrd', meaning fate, so they are creatures of destiny, not mere hags. Holinshed, Shakespeare's source, calls them 'the goddesses of destiny.' Witchcraft was taken seriously and feared as real: King James I, before whom the play was likely performed, had written a book on it, Daemonologie (1597), and his statute of 1604 made witchcraft a capital crime. The sisters' bearded, storm-raising, prophesying magic matches the period's beliefs.
cards.detail_scholar: James's interest was personal: in 1590 a coven at North Berwick was accused of raising storms to wreck the ship bringing him and his bride home from Denmark, and the king examined the suspects himself. Daemonologie defends the reality of witches and their pact with the Devil. Shakespeare's sisters draw on this lore — familiar spirits (Graymalkin the cat, Paddock the toad), the power to sail in a sieve, to raise winds and fog, and to foretell the future — while remaining teasingly ambiguous: they predict but never clearly compel, leaving open how far Macbeth's fall is fate and how far his own choice. The witchcraft would have read as both a topical compliment to the royal author and a genuine menace.

cards.title: Equivocation and the Gunpowder Plot

source.name: The trial of Henry Garnet (1606); the Gunpowder Plot (1605)
source.citation: The Gunpowder Plot, 5 November 1605; the trial and execution of the Jesuit Henry Garnet (1606) for his part in the plot and his defence of equivocation (mental reservation).

cards.summary_basic: The drunken Porter (2.3) imagines admitting to hell 'an equivocator that could swear in both the scales against either scale.' This is topical: in 1605 a Catholic conspiracy, the Gunpowder Plot, tried to blow up King James and Parliament. The Jesuit Henry Garnet, tried in 1606, was notorious for defending 'equivocation' — answering under oath in a deliberately misleading way while privately reserving the true meaning, so as not, technically, to lie. Macbeth later curses 'the equivocation of the fiend / That lies like truth' (5.5).
cards.detail_scholar: Equivocation was a Counter-Reformation doctrine that let persecuted Catholics evade incriminating questions; Garnet had written 'A Treatise of Equivocation,' produced against him at his trial. The technique was infamous by 1606, the year most scholars date the play, making the Porter's joke a sharp contemporary hit. The theme runs through the whole tragedy: the witches are equivocators whose promises 'palter with us in a double sense' (5.8), true to the letter and fatal in the event — 'none of woman born,' a wood that cannot move. Macbeth is destroyed less by lies than by truths he hears wrongly.

cards.title: Touching for the King's Evil

source.name: Holinshed, Chronicles; the royal touch tradition
source.citation: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587); the English royal touch for scrofula ('the King's Evil'), traced to Edward the Confessor (r. 1042-1066) and revived by James I (r. 1603-1625).

cards.summary_basic: In the English scene (4.3), a Doctor describes King Edward the Confessor curing 'the evil' — scrofula, a disfiguring swelling of the lymph nodes long called 'the King's Evil' — by his royal touch, hanging 'a golden stamp' (a coin) about the sufferer's neck. English monarchs were believed to heal scrofula by their touch, taken as a sign of sacred, God-given kingship. The passage flatters King James I, who revived the ceremony, and sets the holy healing king against Macbeth, the murderer who has poisoned his own country.
cards.detail_scholar: The detour is dramatically odd — it has no warrant in Holinshed's Macbeth narrative and halts the action — which is why it reads as a deliberate compliment to the reigning monarch, very possibly performed before James himself. Edward also has 'a heavenly gift of prophecy,' another power the play ties to true, as opposed to demonic, knowledge. The contrast is structural: Act 4 sets England, ruled by a saintly king who cures by touch, against Scotland under a tyrant whose touch is murder, preparing for the restoration of rightful order under Malcolm.

cards.title: Banquo and the Stuart line (the show of kings)

source.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (Scotland), after Hector Boece
source.citation: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), History of Scotland, following Hector Boece; the legendary descent of the Stewart (Stuart) kings from Banquo through his son Fleance.

cards.summary_basic: The witches promise Banquo that, though never king himself, he shall 'get kings' — father a line of them (1.3). In 4.1 they show Macbeth a procession of eight kings, the last holding a glass (mirror) that reveals many more, with Banquo's ghost following to claim them as his descendants. King James I claimed descent from Banquo and Fleance through the royal house of Stuart, so the show flatters the king watching the play: his dynasty is the prophecy's fulfilment, and Macbeth's crimes against Banquo's line are futile.
cards.detail_scholar: The genealogy is legendary, not historical — Banquo and Fleance were probably invented by the chronicler Hector Boece — but the Stuarts embraced the descent, and Shakespeare's audience would have read the eighth king bearing a mirror as James himself, the line stretching past the stage's edge into the present. The 'two-fold balls and treble sceptres' the kings carry (4.1) glance at James's union of crowns: crowned at Scone as King of Scots and at Westminster as King of England, ruler of an enlarged 'Great Britain.' The vision turns Macbeth's tyranny into a doomed assault on the providential founding of the watching king's own dynasty.

cards.title: Harsnett's Declaration and Poor Tom's devils

source.name: Samuel Harsnett, A Declaration of Egregious Popish Impostures (1603)
source.citation: Samuel Harsnett, A Declaration of Egregious Popish Impostures (1603), debunking the fraudulent exorcisms staged by Jesuit priests at Denham, c. 1585-86.

cards.summary_basic: When Edgar disguises himself as the mad beggar 'Poor Tom,' he raves of being possessed by fiends with strange names — Flibbertigibbet, Smulkin, Modo, Mahu, Frateretto. Shakespeare took these names straight from a 1603 book by Samuel Harsnett, A Declaration of Egregious Popish Impostures, which exposed a series of fake exorcisms staged by Catholic priests as cynical frauds. The borrowed devils give Tom's madness a topical, sceptical edge: his 'possession' is a performance, like the exorcisms Harsnett unmasked.
cards.detail_scholar: Harsnett, a Church of England cleric who rose to be Archbishop of York, was commissioned to discredit the Denham exorcisms (c. 1585-86), in which Jesuits claimed to cast demons out of servants. He printed the devils' supposed names and the theatrical tricks used to fake possession. Shakespeare mined the book for Tom's fiends and much of his demonic vocabulary, and the larger irony reverberates through the play: in a tragedy obsessed with what is genuine and what is staged — real madness and feigned, true love and flattery, a real cliff and a fake one — Edgar's counterfeit possession quietly aligns with Harsnett's argument that the spectacular supernatural is so often a human contrivance.

cards.title: King Leir and legendary Britain

source.name: The True Chronicle Historie of King Leir (1605); Geoffrey of Monmouth; Holinshed
source.citation: The True Chronicle Historie of King Leir (anon., printed 1605); Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae (c. 1136); Holinshed, Chronicles (1587); Spenser, The Faerie Queene 2.10.

cards.summary_basic: The Lear story comes from Britain's legendary pre-Roman past, first told by Geoffrey of Monmouth (c. 1136) and retold by Holinshed, Spenser, and an older anonymous play, The True Chronicle Historie of King Leir. In every one of these sources the tale ends happily: Leir is restored to his throne and Cordelia's side wins. Shakespeare's devastating ending — Cordelia hanged, Lear dead of grief — is his own dark invention, a deliberate break with the story his audience knew.
cards.detail_scholar: Geoffrey of Monmouth placed Leir in the legendary line of British kings descended from Brutus of Troy; Holinshed and Spenser passed the story on, and the old King Leir play (acted by 1594, printed 1605) was Shakespeare's closest model. All keep the comforting restoration. By killing Cordelia, Shakespeare violated the received story so painfully that for a century and a half the English stage preferred Nahum Tate's 1681 adaptation, which let Cordelia live and marry Edgar. Samuel Johnson confessed he could hardly bear to re-read the original's last scene. The change is the measure of the play's refusal of consolation.

cards.title: The division of the kingdom and the Union

source.name: The Jacobean debate on the Union of England and Scotland
source.citation: King James I's project to unite England and Scotland as 'Great Britain,' proposed 1604 and debated in Parliament 1604-1607; cf. the doctrine of the unified body politic.

cards.summary_basic: The play opens on Lear dividing Britain among his daughters, tracing the borders on a map. To a Jacobean audience this was a self-evident disaster: a divided kingdom invites rivalry, faction, and civil war — exactly what follows. The folly resonated against current events, for King James I was pressing the opposite case, trying to unite England and Scotland into a single 'Great Britain.' Where James sought to make one realm of two, Lear breaks one realm into three, and the play watches the consequences unfold.
cards.detail_scholar: James, who became King of England in 1603 while remaining King of Scots, urged Parliament from 1604 to merge the two into one 'Great Britain'; the proposal was fiercely debated and ultimately stalled by 1607. Against that backdrop, Lear's partition of the island reads as a cautionary image of the unmaking of a unified body politic. The play's geography insists on it: this is Britain, not a generic kingdom, and the division sets Albany (the old name for Scotland) against Cornwall, dramatizing the fracturing of the very island James hoped to bind together.

cards.title: Dover and the cliff

source.name: The geography of Dover and the Strait of Dover
source.citation: Dover, on the Strait of Dover, the narrowest crossing (about 21 miles) of the English Channel to France; its white chalk cliffs. King Lear 4.6.

cards.summary_basic: Dover is the play's one named place: the white chalk cliffs on the Strait of Dover, where England comes closest to France. It is where Cordelia's French army lands and where everyone converges in Act 4. The blind Gloucester asks to be led to the edge of its famous cliff to throw himself off; his son Edgar, in disguise, paints a dizzying word-picture of the precipice — fishermen like mice, a ship like its own cock-boat — then lets him 'fall' on the flat stage, a staged miracle that shocks him out of despair.
cards.detail_scholar: The choice of Dover is partly strategic — it is the obvious landing-place for a French invasion, and the lords speak of armies converging there — and partly symbolic, the literal edge of the kingdom and of endurance. Edgar's cliff speech (4.6) is a tour de force of theatrical illusion: there is no cliff, only words, and the audience watches a man persuaded to die by description and then saved by the same means. The episode crystallizes the play's preoccupation with seeing and blindness — Gloucester, who 'stumbled when he saw,' must be blind to be led, by a son he cannot recognize, to a fall that is not real.

cards.title: Astrology and the late eclipses

source.name: Renaissance astrology; the eclipses of 1605
source.citation: The lunar eclipse of September 1605 and solar eclipse of October 1605, widely read as portents; the period's debate over astral influence. King Lear 1.2.

cards.summary_basic: Gloucester blames the troubles of the play on 'these late eclipses in the sun and moon,' which 'portend no good to us' (1.2) — astrology was widely believed, and real eclipses in 1605 had stirred just such fears. His bastard son Edmund scornfully rejects it: men blame the stars for vices that are their own choice — 'an admirable evasion of whoremaster man, to lay his goatish disposition to the charge of a star.' The clash sets credulous old belief against a cold new self-reliance, and the play leaves the question of fate and responsibility open.
cards.detail_scholar: Astrology was mainstream learning in Shakespeare's England: almanacs forecast by the stars, and eclipses were read as warnings of disorder in the state. A lunar eclipse in September and a solar eclipse in October 1605 were duly accompanied by alarmed prognostications, making Gloucester's lines topical. Edmund's mockery voices a sceptical, self-authorizing modernity — he makes himself, not the heavens, the author of his deeds — yet the play withholds easy endorsement of either view: Edmund's clear-eyed villainy is monstrous, while Gloucester's fatalism is foolish but humane. The tension feeds the play's larger uncertainty about whether the gods are just, indifferent, or simply absent.

cards.title: The cuckold's horns

source.name: Elizabethan proverbial lore; Ovid, Metamorphoses 3 (Actaeon)
source.citation: The horned cuckold (a man whose wife is unfaithful) was a fixed joke of Elizabethan English, the horns its invisible badge of shame; its mythic emblem is Actaeon, turned into a horned stag (Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.138-252, Golding 1567). Much Ado About Nothing returns to it from Benedick's 'the savage bull's horns ... set them in my forehead' (1.1) to its last scene; cf. The Merry Wives of Windsor 5.5, where Falstaff wears horns as Herne the Hunter.

cards.summary_basic: Elizabethans joked endlessly that a man whose wife was unfaithful (a 'cuckold') sprouted invisible horns on his forehead, a public mark of shame he alone could not see. The fear of being cuckolded, and the anxiety that a wife's faithfulness could never be certain, runs as a nervous joke through the comedy: Benedick swears bachelors alone escape 'the yoke' and the horns, and the threat of cuckoldry shadows even the play's happy ending.
cards.detail_scholar: The horn-joke fuses two ideas: the comic image of the betrayed husband and the older mythic figure of Actaeon, the hunter turned to a horned stag for seeing the goddess Diana bathing, a byword for the man undone by what he sees. In Much Ado the horns are nearly an obsession, with Benedick, Don Pedro, and Claudio trading bull, yoke, and horn jests, and the play's close still turning on it. The same anxiety drives tragedy in Othello and The Winter's Tale, where a husband's groundless certainty of betrayal destroys an innocent wife. The joke encodes a real double standard: a wife's unchastity dishonours her husband, while his shame is figured as something grotesque growing from his own head.

cards.title: 'Nothing': noting, eavesdropping, and the bawdy pun

source.name: Elizabethan pronunciation and wordplay (OED)
source.citation: In Elizabethan English 'nothing' and 'noting' (observing, overhearing, musical notation) were near-homophones; 'nothing' also carried a bawdy sense ('no thing' = the female genitals, against the male 'thing'). The play signposts the pun at 2.3: 'Note this before my notes ... there's not a note of mine that's worth the noting' / 'Notes, notes, forsooth, and nothing!' Cf. OED, 'nothing'; 'note.'

cards.summary_basic: The title is a triple pun. 'Nothing' sounded almost exactly like 'noting' in Shakespeare's England, and 'noting' meant watching, overhearing, and taking note, the eavesdropping that drives every turn of the plot: the loving tricks (Beatrice and Benedick gulled by what they 'note') and the cruel one (Claudio deceived by what he thinks he sees at Hero's window). 'Nothing' was also slang for the female sex, giving the title a bawdy edge: much ado about women, and about a chastity that proves to be 'nothing' amiss.
cards.detail_scholar: Almost everything in the play happens through 'noting': characters hidden in arbours and behind hedges overhear staged conversations; messages are mis-heard and mis-reported; a slander is built on a mis-seen window-scene. The comic plot and the near-tragic plot are the same device turned to opposite ends. The bawdy sense ('nothing' as 'no-thing') sharpens the play's nervousness about female chastity and the cuckold's horns: the 'much ado' is over whether Hero's 'nothing' is intact. Shakespeare plays on the same indecent 'nothing' in Hamlet ('that's a fair thought to lie between maids' legs' ... 'Nothing') and in King Lear's 'Nothing will come of nothing.'

cards.title: A woman's honour: chastity and the double standard

source.name: Juan Luis Vives, The Instruction of a Christian Woman (1523; Eng. 1529)
source.citation: Renaissance conduct literature held that a woman's honour was identical with her chastity, while a man's lay in valour and reputation: Juan Luis Vives, De institutione feminae christianae (1523), trans. Richard Hyrde as The Instruction of a Christian Woman (1529); cf. the period commonplace that a woman has 'nothing to be honest with but her chastity.'

cards.summary_basic: In Shakespeare's world a respectable woman's whole honour rested on her chastity: virginity before marriage and absolute faithfulness within it. A man's honour, by contrast, lay in courage and good name and was not destroyed by his own sexual conduct. Because a single accusation of unchastity, true or false, could ruin a woman and her family, Hero's public shaming at the altar is treated as a kind of social death, and her own father at first wishes her truly dead.
cards.detail_scholar: Conduct books such as Vives's, widely read in Tudor England, taught that chastity was a woman's defining and almost only essential virtue. The asymmetry is brutal and explicit in Much Ado: Claudio and Don Pedro disgrace Hero on the strength of one night-time glimpse, while no comparable charge could touch them; Leonato half-believes the accusation at once because the stakes of female 'honour' make even a father assume the worst. The same code turns lethal in Othello and The Winter's Tale and underlies the bed-trick plays Measure for Measure and All's Well That Ends Well. Beatrice's furious 'O God, that I were a man!' (4.1) is a protest against a world in which she cannot defend her cousin herself.

cards.title: The constable and the night watch

source.name: William Lambarde, The Duties of Constables, Borsholders, Tithingmen (1582)
source.citation: The unpaid parish constable and his night watch were the lowest rung of Elizabethan local law-enforcement; their offices and (often mocked) limits are set out in William Lambarde's handbook The Duties of Constables, Borsholders, Tithingmen, and such other low Ministers of the Peace (1582). Dogberry is a 'constable' and Verges a 'headborough' (= borsholder); the comparable figure is Constable Elbow in Measure for Measure.

cards.summary_basic: Everyday policing in Shakespeare's England was done by ordinary householders serving in turn, without pay or training, as parish constables and watchmen. They were proverbially old, timid, and inept, and were told to make as little trouble as possible. Dogberry, the self-important constable of Messina, and his deputy Verges, a 'headborough,' are Shakespeare's affectionate satire of these amateur officers, whose bungling watch nonetheless stumbles onto the truth and saves Hero.
cards.detail_scholar: Lambarde's manual lays out the constable's and headborough's duties — keeping watch, arresting vagrants and 'nightwalkers,' presenting offenders — the very tasks Dogberry garbles in his charge to the Watch (3.3: 'you shall comprehend all vagrom men'). His speech is a tissue of malapropisms (using a wrong word that sounds like the intended one, often its opposite: 'comprehend' for apprehend, 'auspicious' for suspicious), the comic device later named for Mrs Malaprop in Sheridan's The Rivals (1775). The joke that justice arrives in spite of, not because of, its officers is sharpened by the real reputation of the watch; Shakespeare drew the same comedy from Constable Dull in Love's Labour's Lost and Elbow in Measure for Measure.

cards.title: Twelfth Night and the Lord of Misrule

source.name: Philip Stubbes, The Anatomie of Abuses (1583); the Roman Saturnalia
source.citation: Twelfth Night (5-6 January, the eve and feast of the Epiphany) was the climax of the twelve days of Christmas, a season of feasting and inverted order presided over by a mock 'Lord of Misrule' — described disapprovingly in Philip Stubbes, The Anatomie of Abuses (1583). The festival descends from the Roman midwinter Saturnalia, when masters served slaves and a mock king reigned.

cards.summary_basic: The play is named for the holiday of Twelfth Night, the riotous close of the Christmas season, when households crowned a 'Lord of Misrule' to preside over feasting, disguising, and a topsy-turvy world in which the usual order was turned upside down. The play enacts that festive inversion: a woman rules as a page, a steward dreams of marrying his mistress, a fool is the wisest person on stage, and 'cakes and ale' defy sober authority — a licence that, like the holiday, must finally end.
cards.detail_scholar: The subtitle 'What You Will' signals holiday licence: do as you like. The Christmas Lord of Misrule (the 'Abbot of Unreason'; in France the 'Feast of Fools') and the ancient Saturnalia behind him institutionalised a brief, sanctioned overturning of hierarchy. Sir Toby's defence of 'cakes and ale' against Malvolio's sobriety is the play's manifesto of misrule; but festive inversion is temporary by definition, and the comedy darkens as the holiday wanes — Malvolio is genuinely abused, and Feste's closing song turns from holiday to the everyday world where 'the rain it raineth every day.'

cards.title: Puritanism and revelry ('a kind of Puritan')

source.name: Philip Stubbes, The Anatomie of Abuses (1583)
source.citation: Puritans were the strict, reforming wing of English Protestantism, known for sober dress, sabbath-keeping, and hostility to festivity, music, and the stage — attitudes attacked and embodied in Philip Stubbes, The Anatomie of Abuses (1583). In Twelfth Night 2.3 Maria calls the killjoy steward Malvolio 'a kind of Puritan,' and his clash with Sir Toby is the play's holiday-versus-sobriety quarrel.

cards.summary_basic: 'Puritan' was a (usually hostile) name for strict Protestants who frowned on revelry, ornament, music, dancing, and especially the theatre. Maria calls Malvolio 'a kind of Puritan' for his sour disapproval of the household's late-night fun. Malvolio is no clergyman but the type of the self-righteous killjoy, and the comedy pits his cold sobriety against Sir Toby's festive 'cakes and ale' — then punishes him for it.
cards.detail_scholar: Puritans were prominent opponents of the public theatres (which they would help close in 1642), so a stage-Puritan was an easy and pointed target for a company of players. Maria at once qualifies her label: Malvolio is no true Puritan but 'a time-pleaser,' a self-loving social climber whose 'Puritanism' is really vanity. The portrait is double-edged — his priggishness is mocked, but his cruel gulling and imprisonment as a madman give him a genuine grievance, and his exit line, 'I'll be revenged on the whole pack of you,' has been read as a foretaste of the resentment that would shut the theatres a generation later.

cards.title: Illyria

source.name: Classical geography (Pliny, Natural History); Roman Illyricum
source.citation: Illyria was the ancient name for the eastern Adriatic coast (roughly modern Croatia, Montenegro, and Albania), the Roman province of Illyricum. Famous in antiquity for its pirates (cf. Pliny, Natural History 3.21-26 on the region), it was for Shakespeare's audience a remote, half-romantic, sea-girt land. Twelfth Night is set there, washing Viola ashore among strangers.

cards.summary_basic: Illyria was a real but, to the English, remote and exotic land on the far side of the Adriatic Sea, with an ancient reputation for shipwreck and piracy. Shakespeare uses it as a romance-world: a place reached by shipwreck, where a stranded girl can reinvent herself, where a 'notable pirate' like Antonio may be an old enemy of the duke, and where ordinary rules are pleasantly suspended.
cards.detail_scholar: Shakespeare needed a coast both real enough to be plausible and distant enough to be magical; the Adriatic Illyria, known mainly from classical geography and its piratical past, served perfectly. The name may also have carried for an attentive ear a faint echo of 'illusion' or 'delirium,' suiting a play of disguises and mistakings. Its seaboard setting is essential to the plot: the sea both separates the twins (the shipwreck) and restores them (Sebastian's and Antonio's arrival by sea).

cards.title: Pastoral and the Forest of Arden

source.name: Lodge, Rosalynde (1590); the classical and Renaissance pastoral
source.citation: Thomas Lodge, Rosalynde: Euphues' Golden Legacy (1590) — the prose romance Shakespeare dramatized; behind it the classical pastoral of Theocritus's Idylls (3rd c. BCE) and Virgil's Eclogues (c. 39 BCE), and the Renaissance Arcadias of Sannazaro (1504) and Sidney (1590). 'Arden' is at once the Ardennes of Lodge's tale and Shakespeare's own Warwickshire forest (and his mother's maiden name, Mary Arden).

cards.summary_basic: Pastoral is an old literary mode in which courtiers and poets imagine a simplified country world of shepherds, song, and love, used to hold up a mirror to the corruption of court and city. As You Like It is Shakespeare's fullest pastoral, sending its exiles into the Forest of Arden — a 'green world' where rank relaxes and identities can be remade — while gently mocking the convention even as it delights in it.
cards.detail_scholar: The play follows the green-world pattern Shakespeare also uses in A Midsummer Night's Dream and The Winter's Tale: characters flee a hostile court into a forest where confusions are worked out, then return renewed. It keeps a knowing double vision — the 'real' shepherd Corin, who earns what he eats, set against the literary lovers Silvius and Phebe; Touchstone's deflation of country life in his debate with Corin (3.2); and Jaques's sourness pricking the idyll. Lodge's Rosalynde supplies the plot almost entire; Shakespeare adds Touchstone, Jaques, Audrey, and William.

cards.title: Robin Hood and the greenwood

source.name: The medieval Robin Hood ballads
source.citation: The English outlaw ballads and A Gest of Robyn Hode (printed c. 1500): the greenwood tradition of Robin Hood and his 'merry men' living free under the trees of Sherwood, outside a corrupt law. In As You Like It 1.1 Duke Senior is reported to live in Arden 'like the old Robin Hood of England... and fleet the time carelessly, as they did in the golden world.'

cards.summary_basic: Robin Hood was the legendary English outlaw who, with his band of 'merry men,' lived freely in the greenwood — Sherwood Forest — beyond the reach of a corrupt authority, hunting the king's deer and feasting under the trees. It was a folk-image of liberty, fellowship, and rough justice. Duke Senior's company of banished lords in Arden is explicitly likened to Robin Hood's, which gives the forest its festive, golden, outlaw-utopia colouring.
cards.detail_scholar: The greenwood is a place of misrule and renewal, an escape from court hierarchy into fellowship — the same imaginative space the foresters share with the Lord of Misrule and the golden world. The tradition also stands directly behind the band of banished gentlemen-outlaws in The Two Gentlemen of Verona (4.1), who want Valentine for their 'king' and claim to live as honourably as 'the old Robin Hood of Sherwood.' The image lets a comedy treat exile as holiday rather than catastrophe.

cards.title: The seven ages of man and the world as a stage

source.name: The ages-of-man topos; the theatrum mundi
source.citation: The classical-medieval division of a human life into 'ages' (Hippocrates and Ptolemy gave seven, linked to the seven planets); the theatrum mundi or 'world as a stage' commonplace (John of Salisbury, Policraticus 3.8, 1159), echoed in the Globe theatre's reputed motto 'Totus mundus agit histrionem' — 'all the world plays the actor.' In As You Like It 2.7 the melancholy Jaques delivers 'All the world's a stage, / And all the men and women merely players.'

cards.summary_basic: Jaques's most famous speech weaves together two old ideas: that the world is a vast theatre in which every person plays an assigned part, and that a life divides into a fixed series of 'ages.' He counts seven — mewling infant, whining schoolboy, sighing lover, quarrelsome soldier, well-fed justice, lean slippered 'pantaloon,' and finally 'second childishness and mere oblivion, / Sans teeth, sans eyes, sans taste, sans everything.' A comic set-piece turns into a bleak survey of a whole life.
cards.detail_scholar: Schemes of the ages of man were a schoolroom commonplace, sometimes mapped onto the seven planets (Ptolemy's Tetrabiblos); the theatrum mundi was a Renaissance favourite, lending the Globe its supposed motto. Jaques's version is mordant, stripping each stage of dignity and ending in decay — but Shakespeare answers it at once with the entrance of the faithful old Adam, carried in starving but loved, a living rebuttal of 'sans everything.' The world-as-stage recurs across the canon, from Macbeth's 'poor player' to Lear's 'great stage of fools.'

cards.title: Melancholy and the malcontent

source.name: Galenic humoral theory; Bright, A Treatise of Melancholie (1586)
source.citation: The ancient theory of the four humours (Galen, after Hippocrates): an excess of black bile (Greek melan chole, 'black bile') makes one 'melancholy.' Timothy Bright, A Treatise of Melancholie (1586), and later Robert Burton, The Anatomy of Melancholy (1621), are the great English studies. In As You Like It the lord Jaques is the type of the fashionable malcontent, who 'can suck melancholy out of a song as a weasel sucks eggs' (2.5).

cards.summary_basic: Elizabethans believed temperament was ruled by four bodily 'humours'; an excess of black bile produced melancholy — sadness, brooding, and detachment. By 1600 the melancholy man had become a stage fashion, the 'malcontent': a witty, disillusioned outsider who stands apart and rails at the world's folly. Jaques is Shakespeare's gentlest example — all mournful wit and no real malice, who cultivates his sadness as a pose and prizes his own 'humorous sadness.'
cards.detail_scholar: The four humours (blood/sanguine, phlegm/phlegmatic, yellow bile/choleric, black bile/melancholic) were thought to govern health and character. The malcontent — a fashionable, travelled, often satirical melancholic — was a recognizable type (Marston's Malevole, Webster's Bosola, and, far darker, Hamlet and the bastard Don John of Much Ado). Jaques wears the costume lightly: his melancholy is 'compounded of many simples,' a connoisseur's affectation that the play both enjoys and quietly judges, leaving him to withdraw from the weddings he cannot share.

cards.title: Renaissance friendship and the friend-versus-love ideal

source.name: Cicero, De Amicitia; Elyot, The Boke Named the Governour (1531)
source.citation: Cicero, De Amicitia (44 BCE); the tale of Titus and Gisippus (Boccaccio, Decameron 10.8), retold in Sir Thomas Elyot's The Boke Named the Governour (1531), Book 2, where one friend yields his own betrothed to the other; the classical exemplum of Damon and Pythias. In The Two Gentlemen of Verona 5.4 Valentine, on Proteus's repentance, offers 'All that was mine in Silvia I give thee.'

cards.summary_basic: Renaissance humanists prized male friendship (Latin amicitia) as the highest of bonds — higher, in the most extreme tellings, than romantic love. In the popular tale of Titus and Gisippus, one friend even surrenders his bride to the other. This ideal lies behind Valentine's startling offer to give Silvia to the very friend who has just betrayed and tried to force her — a gesture that has divided audiences for centuries.
cards.detail_scholar: Cicero's De Amicitia and stories like Damon and Pythias and Titus and Gisippus made self-sacrificing friendship a moral commonplace; Elyot's Governour held it up for English readers. The play stages friendship and love in collision — two gentlemen, two ladies — and resolves it with Valentine's amicitia-driven offer, which modern audiences find shocking because it seems to treat Silvia as a transferable token (she is given no line in response). Shakespeare returns to the friend-versus-love tension in The Merchant of Venice (Antonio and Bassanio) and in the rival-kinsmen plot of The Two Noble Kinsmen.
